Stability-Audited, Explainable Machine Learning for Diagnostic Triage of Referred Patients with Liver Disease (ILPD cohort)¶

A leakage-free, reproducible analysis — revised after peer review (nested repeated CV · equivalence testing · calibration · decision curves · SHAP/XAI with controls · stability audit · simulation)¶

How to read this notebook. Every step is followed by a compact block: Why (the reason it is done) · Effect (what it changes in the results) · Advantage (what it buys scientifically) · Trade-off (the honest cost). Section order follows a journal manuscript: Data → Design → Sensitivity → Performance → Calibration & utility → Explainability → Stability → Simulation → Limitations → Reporting checklist.

Revision note. This version responds to a referee report. The principal changes are: (i) the problem is framed as diagnostic triage in a referral population (71 % prevalence), not population screening; (ii) the primary pipeline uses no resampling (SMOTE-NC for all seven learners and class weights for all seven learners are sensitivity analyses); (iii) learner parity is judged with equivalence tests and ΔAUC intervals, and boosting models receive a much larger tuning budget; (iv) calibration is reported with CIs and the recalibration design is examined; (v) the XAI faithfulness test now has competing rankings and a retrain-without-feature (ROAR) control; (vi) the stability audit has null/benchmark scales and a family-level analysis; (vii) clinical baselines, an interpretable-by-design model, odds ratios and a sample-size calculation are added; (viii) a leakage replication tests the claim about published ILPD accuracies; (ix) a simulation study with known ground truth tests whether the conclusions generalise.

Abstract (all numbers are produced by the cells below). Background. Routine blood tests are an attractive basis for triaging patients referred with suspected liver disease, but public benchmarks such as the Indian Liver Patient Dataset (ILPD) are small, prevalence-enriched (71 % liver patients) and are usually judged on a single data split with unaudited explanations. Methods. 566 de-duplicated ILPD patients (404 liver patients, 162 non-liver). Seven learners (logistic regression, RF, ExtraTrees, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, RBF-SVM) were compared in a leakage-free pipeline (log-transform and standardisation inside folds; no resampling in the primary analysis, SMOTE-NC and class weights as sensitivity analyses) under repeated nested cross-validation (5 × 3 outer folds, 3-fold inner tuning by AUC, threshold and Platt re-calibration from 10-fold cross-fitted predictions). Learner parity was judged with ΔAUC intervals and TOST equivalence tests; the boosting models and SVM also received a 4–6-fold larger tuning budget. Explanations (SHAP, grouped permutation, PDP/ICE, deletion and retrain-without-feature tests against competing rankings) were audited against null and benchmark references. Five further public datasets and a simulation with known ground truth tested whether the conclusions generalise, and a leakage replication tested how published ILPD accuracies can arise. Results. Nested-CV AUC was 0.749 (95 % CI 0.686–0.812) for logistic regression, 0.750 (0.684–0.816) for ExtraTrees, 0.739 for RF, 0.738 for CatBoost, 0.722 for XGBoost, 0.720 for LightGBM and 0.685 (0.607–0.763) for the SVM. LR and ET were equivalent within ±0.03 AUC (ΔAUC −0.001, 95 % CI −0.018 to +0.016; TOST p = 0.001). The data were compatible with LR–RF and LR–CatBoost differences of up to ≈ 0.03–0.04 (equivalence shown at ±0.05 only); equivalence with XGBoost, LightGBM and the SVM could not be shown (LR − XGBoost +0.027, CI −0.003 to +0.056; LR − SVM +0.064, CI +0.005 to +0.123, Holm p = 0.21). A 6-fold larger search did not improve XGBoost, LightGBM or CatBoost (ΔAUC −0.007 to 0.000). SMOTE-NC or class weights changed AUC by ≤ 0.008 for six of seven learners (all unadjusted p ≥ 0.30); the SVM was the exception (+0.068 with either, unadjusted p = 0.03). Total bilirubin alone gave AUC 0.699; the full LR improved on it by 0.050 (95 % CI 0.009–0.091), a four-marker LR reached 0.739. After re-calibration the LR slope was 0.92 (0.72–1.16). At the cohort's own prevalence the models gave net benefit over “treat all” only at thresholds ≥ 0.6; under a hypothetical prior shift to 20 % or 5 % prevalence they did so over wide ranges, which is a property of the prevalence, not evidence of screening utility. AUC was 0.635 in women and 0.771 in men (ΔAUC 0.136, 0.040–0.248, Holm p = 0.028), without a significant sex × marker interaction (omnibus p = 0.78). The original single split (AUC 0.836 for LR) lay at the 98.5th percentile of 200 splits (mean 0.754, SD 0.041). In the leakage replication, applying SMOTE-ENN to the whole dataset before cross-validation inflated accuracy to 0.91–0.95 (AUC 0.95–0.99) against 0.62–0.73 for the leakage-free pipeline. SHAP rankings agreed with permutation (ρ = 0.93) and univariate AUC (ρ = 0.93) and beat random removal, but were not better than these competing rankings. Under bootstrap resampling the ExtraTrees SHAP ranking had mean pairwise ρ = 0.76 (label-permuted null 0.04; LR benchmark 0.85), 0.89 at the level of clinical feature families (bilirubin first in 94 % of replicates). Across five public datasets the pooled LR − ET difference was −0.003 (−0.015 to +0.010) and SMOTE changed AUC by −0.002 (−0.004 to +0.001); in a simulation with known truth the nested-CV AUC bias was ≤ 0.004, but TOST declared equivalence at ±0.03 in only 4–42 % of replicates even though the true differences were that small. Conclusion. In this referral cohort routine laboratory data support moderate discrimination (AUC ≈ 0.75). A transparent logistic model is equivalent to ExtraTrees within ±0.03 AUC and not detectably worse than the other ensembles, but the study is under-powered to prove parity with the boosting models, subgroup performance is weaker in women, calibrated probabilities do not transport to screening prevalence, and fine-grained feature rankings are not stable. The single-dataset findings are consistent with, but do not by themselves establish, the pattern seen on five public datasets and in simulation.

0. What was wrong with the original notebook, and what this version changes¶

A Q1 reviewer would flag the following issues in the submitted model.ipynb. Each is fixed here and the fix is justified in the section noted.

# Issue in the original Why a reviewer objects Fix in this notebook §
1 Hyper-parameter search scored roc_auc_score(y, (p >= t)) — AUC of an already-binarised prediction (comments say "F1") Not a probability-ranking AUC; it equals balanced accuracy, so the "inner F1/AUC" is mislabelled and the search criterion is noisy Hyper-parameters are chosen by threshold-free inner AUC; the threshold is chosen in a separate step 5
2 Headline result = one 80/20 split (n_test = 114), AUC 0.83 A single split is not evidence; its CI is about ±0.09 and the value can be lucky Primary estimate = repeated nested CV (15 outer folds); the single split is kept only as a diagnostic, located in the distribution of 200 random splits (§8) 5, 8
3 All 6 models were scored on the hold-out test set before the final model was chosen Test-set peeking → optimistic selection Test data are never used for selection; model choice comes from nested CV only 5
4 SMOTE interpolates the binary Gender column (e.g. 0.37 "gender") Produces impossible patients SMOTE-NC (nominal-continuous) keeps Gender binary 3
5 Heavily right-skewed lab values (TB, DB, ALP, SGPT, SGOT) enter linear/kernel models and SMOTE distance un-transformed Distances dominated by outliers log1p + standardisation inside the pipeline 2, 3
6 Feature-selection by RF-importance inside every model with 10 features, never ablated Adds variance; confounds the model comparison Tested in an ablation; dropped because it gave no gain 4
7 No simple baseline (logistic regression) and no trivial baseline Without it "ML beats X" is meaningless on a 10-feature clinical table Logistic regression + prevalence baseline added 5
8 No uncertainty / no significance tests between models Differences of 0.01 AUC are noise at n = 566 Nadeau–Bengio corrected paired tests + Holm correction 6
9 SMOTE-trained probabilities are not calibrated; no calibration or clinical-utility analysis Clinical journals require it (TRIPOD+AI) Nested Platt re-calibration, calibration slope, decision-curve analysis 7
10 No explainability, no stability analysis The two things you asked for SHAP + permutation + PDP/ICE; four-level stability audit 9–11

1. Set-up and reproducibility¶

Why. Journals (and TRIPOD+AI item 9) require that another group can re-run the study and obtain the same numbers. All randomness flows from one SEED; library versions are printed; all heavy computations are cached on disk keyed by their configuration.
Effect. None on accuracy; it removes "it works on my machine" and run-to-run drift.
Advantage. Exact reproducibility + an audit trail (environment table below can be pasted into the Methods section).
Trade-off. Cached results must be deleted (cache/) if code changes.

2. Data, cohort flow and descriptive statistics¶

2.1 Loading, cleaning and cohort flow¶

Why. (i) 4 records lack the albumin/globulin ratio (0.7 %) and 13 records are exact duplicates. Duplicates must be removed before any split: otherwise the same patient lands in both train and test folds and inflates every metric. (ii) With 0.7 % missing, complete-case analysis introduces negligible bias; imputation would add modelling choices without measurable benefit.
Effect. 583 → 566 patients. Class balance is essentially unchanged (71.4 % disease).
Advantage. No leakage via duplicates; a reportable cohort-flow (TRIPOD+AI item 12).
Trade-off. The dataset has no patient ID, so we cannot exclude that non-identical repeated visits of one patient exist; this is listed under Limitations.

2.2 "Table 1" — cohort characteristics by class, with univariate discrimination¶

Why. Every clinical-ML paper opens with Table 1. Univariate AUC and a multiplicity-adjusted Mann–Whitney test show which single markers carry signal; this is the reference against which the SHAP ranking is sanity-checked later (§9).
Effect. None on modelling; provides face-validity (e.g. bilirubin, ALP and transaminases should be higher in liver patients, albumin lower).
Advantage. Non-parametric (lab values are skewed) and FDR-corrected (Benjamini–Hochberg), so the table does not over-claim.

In [3]:
rows = []
pos, neg = d[d.target==1], d[d.target==0]
for f in FEATURES:
    if f == "Gender":
        a, b = pos[f].mean()*100, neg[f].mean()*100
        u, p = stats.mannwhitneyu(pos[f], neg[f]); auc = u/(len(pos)*len(neg))
        rows.append([ "Male sex, %", f"{a:.1f}", f"{b:.1f}", p, auc])
    else:
        q = lambda s: f"{s.median():.1f} [{s.quantile(.25):.1f}–{s.quantile(.75):.1f}]"
        u, p = stats.mannwhitneyu(pos[f], neg[f]); auc = u/(len(pos)*len(neg))
        rows.append([f, q(pos[f]), q(neg[f]), p, auc])
t1 = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Variable", f"Liver patients (n={len(pos)})", f"Non-liver (n={len(neg)})", "p_raw", "Univariate AUC"])
# direction-corrected AUC: AUC of the marker oriented so that 'higher = more liver-like' (albumin and A/G ratio are LOWER in liver patients)
t1["Oriented AUC"] = np.maximum(t1["Univariate AUC"], 1 - t1["Univariate AUC"]).round(3)
t1["Higher in"] = np.where(t1["Univariate AUC"] >= .5, "liver patients", "non-liver")
t1["p_FDR"] = stats.false_discovery_control(t1.p_raw.values)
t1["Univariate AUC"] = t1["Univariate AUC"].round(3)
t1["p_raw"] = t1.p_raw.map(lambda v: f"{v:.1e}"); t1["p_FDR"] = t1.p_FDR.map(lambda v: f"{v:.1e}")
t1.to_csv(TAB/"table1_cohort.csv", index=False)
t1.set_index("Variable")

2.3 Distribution and collinearity checks → design decisions¶

Why. Two properties of the data drive the preprocessing: (a) strong right-skew in five enzyme/bilirubin variables, (b) strong correlation inside clinical families (bilirubins, transaminases, protein/albumin). (a) justifies a log1p transform; (b) is critical for XAI because SHAP and permutation importance split or hide credit between correlated features — so we will also report grouped importance (§9).
Effect. Skewness drops to |skew| < 1.5 after log1p (see table). Trees are invariant to monotone transforms, but LR/SVM and SMOTE's k-NN distances are not.
Advantage. Evidence-based preprocessing and a-priori feature groups instead of ad-hoc ones.

Xl = X.copy(); Xl[LOG_COLS] = np.log1p(Xl[LOG_COLS])
rho = Xl.corr(method="spearman")
def vif(df):
    Z = (df - df.mean())/df.std(); out = {}
    for c in df.columns:
        o = np.linalg.lstsq(Z.drop(columns=c).values, Z[c].values, rcond=None); res = Z[c].values - Z.drop(columns=c).values @ o[0]
        out[c] = 1/(res.var()/Z[c].var())
    return pd.Series(out)
VIF = vif(Xl).round(1)

3. Study design and the leakage-free modelling pipeline¶

3.1 The pipeline (everything that "learns from data" lives inside the cross-validation loop)¶

log1p (5 skewed labs) → StandardScaler → classifier (primary; SMOTE-NC or class weights are added only in the sensitivity analyses of §6.2)

Component Why Effect Advantage Trade-off
log1p + standardise skewed labs; k-NN (SMOTE) and LR/SVM are scale-sensitive stabilises LR/SVM coefficients/kernels, no change for trees one pipeline works for all 7 learners → fair comparison log scale changes how coefficients read (per log-unit)
Imbalance handling: none (primary) 71 %/29 % imbalance, but AUC is prevalence-free and the threshold is tuned separately; published evidence ([34, 35] in the manuscript) and our own ablation show resampling adds no AUC and distorts calibration probabilities stay on the natural prevalence scale no synthetic data, no probability distortion, fewer moving parts the default 0.5 cut-off favours the majority class → the threshold is chosen in a nested step (§5)
SMOTE-NC / class weights (sensitivity) SMOTE-NC (inside the pipeline, Gender kept binary) and class weights are run for all seven learners (§6.2) shifts probabilities and the 0.5 operating point applied only on training folds by imblearn.Pipeline; tests that conclusions do not depend on the primary choice tripled computation
Classifier zoo LR (transparent baseline), RF, ET, XGB, LGBM, CAT, SVM — covers linear, bagging, boosting, kernel families more models → more multiplicity; handled by corrected tests (§6)

Minority class here is non-liver (label 0), because the dataset's positive class (liver patient) is the majority. Throughout, positive = liver patient, so sensitivity = detecting liver disease and specificity = correctly clearing a non-liver patient.

In [5]:
N_POS_NEG = (y==0).sum()/(y==1).sum()                      # class ratio used only for XGBoost's cost-sensitive option

def make_pre(log=True):
    lg = FunctionTransformer(np.log1p if log else None, feature_names_out="one-to-one")
    return ColumnTransformer([("lg", Pipeline([("f", lg), ("s", StandardScaler())]), LOG_COLS),
                              ("num", StandardScaler(), NUM_COLS),
                              ("cat", "passthrough", CAT_COLS)], verbose_feature_names_out=False)

from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, ClassifierMixin
from scipy.special import expit
class SVCDec(BaseEstimator, ClassifierMixin):
    # RBF-SVM whose score is sigmoid(decision_function). The single Platt step is done by the nested pipeline; this avoids
    # SVC(probability=True), which runs its own internal 5-fold Platt scaling underneath ours (unstable on n~450, not rank-consistent).
    def __init__(self, C=1.0, gamma="scale", class_weight=None, random_state=None):
        self.C, self.gamma, self.class_weight, self.random_state = C, gamma, class_weight, random_state
    def fit(self, X_, y_):
        self.m_ = SVC(C=self.C, gamma=self.gamma, class_weight=self.class_weight, probability=False, random_state=self.random_state).fit(X_, y_); self.classes_ = self.m_.classes_; return self
    def predict_proba(self, X_):
        p = expit(self.m_.decision_function(X_)); return np.c_[1-p, p]

def build_clf(name, imb="smote", seed=SEED):
    cw = (imb == "cw")
    if name == "LR":   return LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000, class_weight="balanced" if cw else None)
    if name == "RF":   return RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=seed, n_jobs=1, class_weight="balanced" if cw else None)
    if name == "ET":   return ExtraTreesClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=seed, n_jobs=1, class_weight="balanced" if cw else None)
    if name == "XGB":  return XGBClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=seed, n_jobs=1, eval_metric="logloss", scale_pos_weight=N_POS_NEG if cw else 1.0)
    if name == "LGBM": return LGBMClassifier(random_state=seed, n_jobs=1, verbose=-1, class_weight="balanced" if cw else None)
    if name == "CAT":  return CatBoostClassifier(iterations=300, verbose=0, random_seed=seed, thread_count=1, auto_class_weights="Balanced" if cw else None)
    if name == "SVM":  return SVCDec(random_state=seed, class_weight="balanced" if cw else None)
    raise KeyError(name)

def make_pipe(name, imb="smote", log=True, select=False, seed=SEED):
    steps = [("pre", make_pre(log))]
    if imb == "smote":
        steps.append(("smote", SMOTENC(categorical_features=[len(FEATURES)-1], k_neighbors=5, random_state=seed)))
    if select:
        from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectFromModel
        steps.append(("sel", SelectFromModel(RandomForestClassifier(200, random_state=0, n_jobs=1), threshold="median")))
    steps.append(("clf", build_clf(name, imb, seed)))
    return Pipeline(steps)

3.2 Evaluation protocol (what is estimated, by what, and why)¶

Layer Procedure Why Effect Advantage
Outer loop 5-fold stratified CV × 3 repeats (15 test folds, every patient tested 3×) n = 566 is small; one split has ±0.07 AUC uncertainty variance of the estimate falls, and its spread becomes reportable (stability!) unbiased performance for the whole procedure (tuning + threshold + SMOTE)
Inner loop 3-fold stratified CV, 25 random hyper-parameter candidates, criterion = mean inner AUC selection must never see outer-test data; AUC is threshold-free and prevalence-free removes the bug in the original (AUC of binarised predictions) smooth, low-variance selection criterion
Threshold after picking hyper-parameters, the selected configuration is cross-fitted with 10-fold CV on the outer-training data and the cut-off maximising smoothed balanced accuracy (= Youden-J) is chosen on those out-of-fold probabilities with a prevalence of 71 % the 0.5 cut-off is arbitrary; balanced accuracy weights sensitivity and specificity equally irrespective of prevalence threshold is data-driven but still nested no outer-test leakage
Re-calibration Platt scaling fitted on the same 10-fold out-of-fold probabilities, applied to the outer test fold scores from AUC-tuned models (and SVM scores) are not probabilities. Cross-fitting with K = 10 (training fraction 90 %) rather than the 3 inner folds (67 %) keeps the calibrator's training-set size close to that of the refitted model; with K = 3 the calibrator over-corrected (§7.1) usable risk estimates for Brier / calibration / decision curves calibration is also estimated out-of-sample; 10 extra fits per outer fold
Statistics Nadeau–Bengio corrected resampled t-test + Holm adjustment fold results share training data → naive t-tests are anti-conservative wider, honest CIs avoids false "winner" claims

4. Sensitivity (ablation) analysis of preprocessing choices¶

Why. Three preprocessing choices were inherited from the original notebook without evidence: class-imbalance handling, log transform and RF-based feature selection. A reviewer will ask whether they matter. We test every combination (3 × 2 × 2 = 12 configurations × 7 models) with default hyper-parameters under 5×3 repeated CV, using a CV seed different from the main study.
Decision rule (stated before looking). A component is kept only if it improves mean AUC across models by more than its Nadeau–Bengio-corrected uncertainty or is neutral and methodologically safer.
Effect. Quantifies how much each choice moves AUC and the sensitivity/specificity balance at the default 0.5 cut-off.
Advantage. Turns design choices into evidence; shows the conclusions do not hinge on one preprocessing recipe.
Trade-off. Selecting the recipe from the same data introduces a small optimism; it is reported, and the choice affects all models equally so model rankings are not biased by it.

In [6]:
ABL_CFGS = [(imb, lg, sel) for imb in ["none","cw","smote"] for lg in [False, True] for sel in [False, True]]

def _abl_job(m, c, splits):
    imb, lg, sel = c; rows = []
    for k, (tr, te) in enumerate(splits):
        p = make_pipe(m, imb=imb, log=lg, select=sel).fit(X.iloc[tr], y.iloc[tr])
        pr = p.predict_proba(X.iloc[te])[:, 1]; yt = y.iloc[te].values; pd_ = (pr >= .5).astype(int)
        tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(yt, pd_, labels=[0,1]).ravel()
        rows.append(dict(model=m, imb=imb, log=lg, sel=sel, fold=k, AUC=roc_auc_score(yt, pr), Sens=tp/(tp+fn), Spec=tn/(tn+fp)))
    return rows

def run_ablation():
    splits = list(RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=CFG["abl_repeats"], random_state=SEED+1).split(X, y))
    out = Parallel(n_jobs=CFG["n_jobs"])(delayed(_abl_job)(m, c, splits) for m in MODELS for c in ABL_CFGS)
    df = pd.DataFrame([r for o in out for r in o]); df["BalAcc"] = (df.Sens + df.Spec)/2; return df
abl = cached("ablation", run_ablation)

def nb_ci(x, ratio=0.25, alpha=0.05):
    # Nadeau & Bengio (2003) corrected resampled CI; ratio = n_test/n_train (=1/4 for 5-fold)
    x = np.asarray(x, float); J = len(x); m = x.mean(); se = np.sqrt((1/J + ratio) * x.var(ddof=1)); t = stats.t.ppf(1-alpha/2, J-1)
    return m, m - t*se, m + t*se
def nb_paired(a, b, ratio=0.25):
    d_ = np.asarray(a, float) - np.asarray(b, float); J = len(d_); se = np.sqrt((1/J + ratio) * d_.var(ddof=1))
    if se == 0: return d_.mean(), 0.0, 1.0
    t = d_.mean()/se; return d_.mean(), t, 2*stats.t.sf(abs(t), J-1)
def holm(p):
    p = np.asarray(p); o = np.argsort(p); adj = np.empty_like(p); run = 0
    for i, idx in enumerate(o):
        run = max(run, (len(p)-i)*p[idx]); adj[idx] = min(1, run)
    return adj

# ---- main effects: marginal mean over models, paired by fold ----
eff = []
for fac, lv_ref, lvls in [("imb", "none", ["none","cw","smote"]), ("log", False, [False, True]), ("sel", False, [False, True])]:
    base = abl[abl[fac]==lv_ref].groupby("fold")[["AUC","BalAcc","Sens","Spec"]].mean()
    for lv in lvls:
        cur = abl[abl[fac]==lv].groupby("fold")[["AUC","BalAcc","Sens","Spec"]].mean()
        m, lo, hi = nb_ci(cur.AUC - base.AUC) if lv != lv_ref else (0, 0, 0)
        eff.append(dict(factor=fac, level=str(lv), AUC=cur.AUC.mean(), dAUC_vs_ref=m, CI95=f"[{lo:+.3f}, {hi:+.3f}]" if lv != lv_ref else "(reference)",
                        BalAcc_at_0p5=cur.BalAcc.mean(), Sens_at_0p5=cur.Sens.mean(), Spec_at_0p5=cur.Spec.mean()))
eff = pd.DataFrame(eff).set_index(["factor","level"]); eff.round(3).to_csv(TAB/"table_ablation_main_effects.csv"); eff.round(3)

Decision taken from §4 (read from the table above).

Component Evidence (marginal mean AUC change vs reference, corrected 95 % CI) Decision
log1p transform 0.000 [−0.007, +0.007] — neutral for AUC Kept. Harmless, scale-stabilises LR/SVM and reduces the influence of outliers.
RF feature selection −0.009 [−0.030, +0.012] — no gain, nominally worse, adds a random component Dropped. Fewer moving parts; 10 features are too few to need selection.
Class weights +0.010 [+0.001, +0.020] — the only nominal AUC gain (borderline; default hyper-parameters; not corrected for multiplicity) Not adopted as primary; re-tested with tuning in §6.2, where the gain disappears for LR and ET.
SMOTE-NC +0.002 [−0.015, +0.019] — no AUC gain; its only effect is to move the 0.5-threshold operating point (sensitivity 0.70 / specificity 0.59 vs 0.88 / 0.27 with no handling) Not adopted as primary (revised after peer review). By the decision rule stated above, AUC does not justify it, and published work [34, 35] and our external datasets (§12.1) show it worsens calibration. It is retained as a sensitivity analysis for all seven learners (§6.2).

The preprocessing used from §5 on is fixed in the PRIMARY dictionary below (no resampling, log1p, no feature selection) so the choice is explicit and auditable.

# >>> Primary recipe (justified by the ablation above and by the sensitivity analysis in 6.2) <<<
PRIMARY = dict(imb="none", log=True, select=False)
print("Primary preprocessing recipe:", PRIMARY)
def pipe_for(name, seed=SEED, **override): return make_pipe(name, seed=seed, **{**PRIMARY, **override})

Primary preprocessing recipe: {'imb': 'none', 'log': True, 'select': False}

5. Nested repeated cross-validation (primary performance estimate)¶

Why. Tuning and evaluating on the same folds yields optimistic scores; nested CV evaluates the entire procedure (preprocessing → hyper-parameter search → threshold selection → calibration; no resampling in the primary pipeline) on data it never touched.
Effect. Typically lowers reported performance relative to non-nested CV — here it also removes the lucky-split effect of the original notebook.
Advantage. The only design that supports an honest, publishable estimate when a separate external cohort is unavailable. Fold-to-fold spread is kept → input for the stability audit (§10).
Trade-off. ≈ 25 candidates × 3 inner folds × 15 outer folds × 7 models fits (cached; runs in parallel).

In [9]:
THR_GRID = np.round(np.arange(0.05, 0.951, 0.01), 2)
def select_threshold(yv, p, k=5):
    # max of a moving-average-smoothed balanced-accuracy curve (smoothing avoids picking a noisy spike)
    curve = np.array([balanced_accuracy_score(yv, p >= t) for t in THR_GRID]); sm = np.convolve(curve, np.ones(k)/k, mode="same")
    i = k//2 + int(np.argmax(sm[k//2:-(k//2)])); return float(THR_GRID[i])
def _logit(p): p = np.clip(p, 1e-6, 1-1e-6); return np.log(p/(1-p)).reshape(-1, 1)
def fit_platt(p, yv): return LogisticRegression(C=1e6, max_iter=1000).fit(_logit(p), yv)

def fold_metrics(yt, p, pc, thr):
    pred = (p >= thr).astype(int); tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(yt, pred, labels=[0,1]).ravel()
    sens, spec = tp/(tp+fn), tn/(tn+fp)
    return dict(AUC=roc_auc_score(yt, p), PR_AUC=average_precision_score(yt, p), Brier=brier_score_loss(yt, pc), BalAcc=(sens+spec)/2,
                Sens=sens, Spec=spec, PPV=tp/(tp+fp) if tp+fp else np.nan, NPV=tn/(tn+fn) if tn+fn else np.nan,
                MCC=matthews_corrcoef(yt, pred), F1=f1_score(yt, pred), Acc=(tp+tn)/len(yt))

def _outer_fold(name, rep, fold, tr, te, cands, seed, recipe=None):
    recipe = recipe or {}
    Xtr, ytr = X.iloc[tr], y.iloc[tr]
    inner = list(StratifiedKFold(CFG["inner_splits"], shuffle=True, random_state=seed).split(Xtr, ytr))
    cand_auc = []
    for prm in cands:                                           # --- inner loop: hyper-parameters by threshold-free AUC ---
        aucs = []
        for a, b in inner:
            m = pipe_for(name, **recipe).set_params(**prm).fit(Xtr.iloc[a], ytr.iloc[a]); aucs.append(roc_auc_score(ytr.iloc[b], m.predict_proba(Xtr.iloc[b])[:, 1]))
        cand_auc.append(np.mean(aucs))
    best = int(np.argmax(cand_auc))
    oof = np.zeros(len(ytr))                                    # --- cross-fit the selected configuration (K = cal_splits) for threshold + calibrator ---
    for a, b in StratifiedKFold(CFG["cal_splits"], shuffle=True, random_state=seed + 1).split(Xtr, ytr):
        oof[b] = pipe_for(name, **recipe).set_params(**cands[best]).fit(Xtr.iloc[a], ytr.iloc[a]).predict_proba(Xtr.iloc[b])[:, 1]
    thr = select_threshold(ytr.values, oof); platt = fit_platt(oof, ytr.values)
    final = pipe_for(name, **recipe).set_params(**cands[best]).fit(Xtr, ytr)                                        # --- refit on outer-train ---
    p = final.predict_proba(X.iloc[te])[:, 1]; pc = platt.predict_proba(_logit(p))[:, 1]
    return dict(model=name, rep=rep, fold=fold, te=te, p=p, pc=pc, thr=thr, best=best, params=cands[best],
                inner_auc=cand_auc[best], cand_auc=np.array(cand_auc), platt=(float(platt.intercept_[0]), float(platt.coef_[0,0])))

def run_nested(name, recipe=None, n_iter=None):
    eff = {**PRIMARY, **(recipe or {})}
    cands = list(ParameterSampler(SPACES[name], n_iter=n_iter or CFG["n_iter"], random_state=SEED))
    if eff["imb"] != "smote":                                         # no SMOTE step -> drop its hyper-parameter
        cands = [{k: v for k, v in c.items() if not k.startswith("smote__")} for c in cands]
    outer = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=CFG["outer_splits"], n_repeats=CFG["outer_repeats"], random_state=SEED)
    jobs = [(i//CFG["outer_splits"], i % CFG["outer_splits"], tr, te) for i, (tr, te) in enumerate(outer.split(X, y))]
    return Parallel(n_jobs=CFG["n_jobs"])(delayed(_outer_fold)(name, r, f, tr, te, cands, SEED + 100*r + f, recipe) for r, f, tr, te in jobs)

NESTED = {m: cached(f"nested_{m}", lambda m=m: run_nested(m)) for m in MODELS}       # primary pipeline: no resampling
rows = []
for m, res in NESTED.items():
    for r in res:
        rows.append(dict(model=m, rep=r["rep"], fold=r["fold"], thr=r["thr"], inner_AUC=r["inner_auc"], **fold_metrics(y.values[r["te"]], r["p"], r["pc"], r["thr"])))
FOLDS = pd.DataFrame(rows); FOLDS.to_csv(TAB/"nested_cv_fold_level.csv", index=False)
print(f"{len(FOLDS)} outer-fold evaluations ({FOLDS.model.nunique()} models x {FOLDS.groupby('model').size().iloc[0]} folds)")

105 outer-fold evaluations (7 models x 15 folds)

5.1 Equalising tuning effort (does "boosting ranked lowest" reflect the learners or the search budget?)¶

Why. Each learner received the same number of random candidates (25), but not the same coverage: for LR the search is two-dimensional and thorough, for XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost (7–11 searched hyper-parameters) 25 draws are sparse. §8.1 also shows a flat inner-AUC landscape and only 20–40 % agreement on the selected candidate, i.e. tuning is partly noise. A learner ranking built on unequal tuning coverage is therefore not trustworthy.
What is done. The complete nested protocol (same outer folds, same inner folds, same threshold/recalibration steps) is re-run with 150 random candidates for XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost and 100 for the SVM (6× / 4× the original budget). The larger search contains the original 25 candidates.
Effect. If the lower AUC of boosting was a search artefact it should rise towards LR/ET.
Advantage. Removes the main confounder of the learner comparison.
Trade-off. Larger searches raise the risk of over-fitting the inner AUC (visible as a larger inner-minus-outer gap, which is reported).

In [10]:
EXT_K = {"XGB": 150, "LGBM": 150, "CAT": 150, "SVM": 100}
EXT = {m: cached(f"nested_ext{k}_{m}", lambda m=m, k=k: run_nested(m, n_iter=k)) for m, k in EXT_K.items()}
def fold_frame(res):
    return pd.DataFrame([dict(rep=r["rep"], fold=r["fold"], thr=r["thr"], inner_AUC=r["inner_auc"], **fold_metrics(y.values[r["te"]], r["p"], r["pc"], r["thr"])) for r in res]).sort_values(["rep", "fold"]).reset_index(drop=True)
FOLDS_EXT = {m: fold_frame(v) for m, v in EXT.items()}

    dd = f.AUC.values - FOLDS_PRIM[m].AUC.values; J = len(dd); se = np.sqrt((1/J + .25)*dd.var(ddof=1)); t95 = stats.t.ppf(.975, J-1)
    ext_rows.append(dict(model=m, candidates=f"25 → {EXT_K[m]}", AUC_25="{:.3f} [{:.3f}, {:.3f}]".format(*nb_ci(FOLDS_PRIM[m].AUC)), AUC_extended="{:.3f} [{:.3f}, {:.3f}]".format(*nb_ci(f.AUC)),
                         delta_AUC=dd.mean(), CI95=f"[{dd.mean()-t95*se:+.3f}, {dd.mean()+t95*se:+.3f}]", inner_AUC_25=FOLDS_PRIM[m].inner_AUC.mean(), inner_AUC_extended=f.inner_AUC.mean(),
                         optimism_ext=(f.inner_AUC - f.AUC).mean()))
EXT_TAB = pd.DataFrame(ext_rows).set_index("model").round(4); EXT_TAB.to_csv(TAB/"table_extended_search.csv"); EXT_TAB

6. Results I — discrimination, classification and formal model comparison¶

Why. Report every metric a clinical reader may want, each with an uncertainty interval that respects the dependence between folds, plus a prevalence-only reference row so readers can see how much better than "predict everyone has liver disease" (accuracy = 71.4 %) the models are.
Effect. Accuracy alone is misleading at 71 % prevalence; AUC, balanced accuracy, MCC and PR-AUC give the complete picture.
Advantage. Corrected CIs and Holm-adjusted tests prevent over-interpreting 0.01–0.02 AUC differences.

In [11]:
METRICS = ["AUC","PR_AUC","BalAcc","Sens","Spec","MCC","Acc","Brier"]

for m in MODELS:

prev = y.mean(); tab["Prevalence baseline"] = dict(AUC="0.500", PR_AUC=f"{prev:.3f}", BalAcc="0.500", Sens="1.000", Spec="0.000", MCC="0.000", Acc=f"{prev:.3f}", Brier=f"{prev*(1-prev):.3f}")
PERF = pd.DataFrame(tab).T[METRICS]; PERF.to_csv(TAB/"table2_nested_cv_performance.csv")
rank_auc = FOLDS.pivot(index=["rep","fold"], columns="model", values="AUC")
fr = stats.friedmanchisquare(*[rank_auc[m] for m in MODELS])
print(f"Friedman test on fold AUC (15 folds, 7 models): chi2={fr.statistic:.2f}, p={fr.pvalue:.3g}   [folds are dependent -> descriptive only]")
print("Mean AUC rank (1 = best):", rank_auc.rank(axis=1, ascending=False).mean().sort_values().round(2).to_dict())

6.1 ROC curves (pooled out-of-fold, averaged over the 3 repeats)¶

Why. ROC shows discrimination across all thresholds, independent of the tuned cut-off.
Effect. The shaded band is the min–max across repeats — a direct visual of partition-to-partition stability.
Advantage. One figure conveys both level and variability of performance.

In [13]:
# pooled out-of-fold predictions per repeat: arrays (R, n)
R = CFG["outer_repeats"]
def pooled(model):
    P, PC, PRED = np.zeros((R, n)), np.zeros((R, n)), np.zeros((R, n), int)
    for r in NESTED[model]:
        P[r["rep"], r["te"]] = r["p"]; PC[r["rep"], r["te"]] = r["pc"]; PRED[r["rep"], r["te"]] = (r["p"] >= r["thr"]).astype(int)
    return P, PC, PRED
POOL = {m: pooled(m) for m in MODELS}
grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
def roc_band(P):
    tprs = []
    for p in P:
        fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y, p); tprs.append(np.interp(grid, fpr, tpr))
    tprs = np.array(tprs); return tprs.mean(0), tprs.min(0), tprs.max(0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 5.2))
for m in sorted(MODELS, key=lambda k: -auc_mean[k]):
    mu, lo, hi = roc_band(POOL[m][0]); hl = m in (BEST, BEST_TREE, "LR")
    ax.plot(grid, mu, color=MCOL[m], lw=2.2 if hl else 1.0, alpha=1 if hl else .6, label=f"{MNAME[m]} (AUC {auc_mean[m]:.3f})")
    if hl: ax.fill_between(grid, lo, hi, color=MCOL[m], alpha=.14, lw=0)
ax.plot([0,1],[0,1], color=GREY, ls=":"); ax.set_xlabel("1 − specificity"); ax.set_ylabel("sensitivity"); ax.set_title("Pooled out-of-fold ROC (mean of 3 repeats)")

6.2 Sensitivity analysis — do the conclusions depend on the imbalance strategy? (all seven learners)¶

Why. The primary pipeline uses no resampling, because (i) the ablation (§4) shows resampling gives no AUC gain, (ii) published simulation work shows resampling distorts calibration without improving discrimination, and (iii) the decision threshold is tuned in a separate nested step, which already removes the need to rebalance the 0.5 cut-off. A reader will nevertheless ask whether the learner comparison is an artefact of that choice. We therefore re-run the entire nested protocol (same folds, same search space and budget, same threshold/recalibration steps) with SMOTE-NC for all seven learners, and with class weights for all seven learners.
Note on the two analyses of class weights. §4 uses default hyper-parameters and a different CV seed and finds class weights +0.010 AUC (marginal mean over learners, CI 0.001–0.020); the nested analysis below tunes hyper-parameters and is the one that matches the final pipeline. The two are different estimands and the table below gives the nested result for each learner.
Effect. If recipes give the same AUC and balanced accuracy after threshold tuning, resampling is unnecessary and the reported performance is a property of the data.
Advantage. Removes the most common objection to SMOTE-based clinical papers and shows whether the learner ranking changes with the recipe.

6.3 Is "no significant difference" equivalence? ΔAUC intervals and TOST¶

Why. A non-significant paired test (Table 3) with 15 correlated folds and SD ≈ 0.055 has little power: the data are compatible with true differences of several hundredths of an AUC. Absence of evidence is not evidence of equivalence. We therefore report (a) the 95 % CI of ΔAUC (LR − learner), (b) a two one-sided test (TOST) against pre-specified margins of ±0.02, ±0.03 and ±0.05 AUC, (c) the smallest margin at which equivalence could be claimed (the half-width of the 90 % CI), and (d) an independent patient-level bootstrap interval of ΔAUC computed on the pooled out-of-fold predictions that does not rely on the fold-based variance formula.
Caveat on the corrected test. The Nadeau–Bengio variance factor (1/J + ntest/ntrain) was derived for random subsampling; applying it to repeated k-fold CV is an approximation that is generally accepted but not exact. The bootstrap interval is provided as a cross-check.
Effect. Turns "indistinguishable" into a quantified bound.
Advantage. Claims about parity are limited to what the data can support. Margins are conventions (0.05 AUC is a commonly cited threshold for a clinically relevant gain), not derived from a utility analysis.

In [15]:
rng_b = np.random.default_rng(SEED); BI = [rng_b.integers(0, n, n) for _ in range(1000)]
def pooled_from(res):
    P, PC = np.zeros((3, n)), np.zeros((3, n))
    for r in res: P[r["rep"], r["te"]] = r["p"]; PC[r["rep"], r["te"]] = r["pc"]
    return P, PC
POOL_SM = {m: pooled_from(v) for m, v in NESTED_SM.items()}
def tost_p(dm, se, J, margin): return max(stats.t.sf((dm + margin)/se, J-1), stats.t.cdf((dm - margin)/se, J-1))
def eq_table(F, P, label, ref="LR"):
    rows_ = []
    for m in [k for k in MODELS if k != ref]:
        dd = F[ref].AUC.values - F[m].AUC.values; J = len(dd); se = np.sqrt((1/J + .25)*dd.var(ddof=1)); dm = dd.mean(); t95, t90 = stats.t.ppf(.975, J-1), stats.t.ppf(.95, J-1)
        pa, pb = P[ref][0].mean(0), P[m][0].mean(0); bs = np.array([roc_auc_score(y.values[i], pa[i]) - roc_auc_score(y.values[i], pb[i]) for i in BI[:600]])
        rows_.append(dict(recipe=label, comparison=f"{ref} − {m}", dAUC=dm, CI95_NB=f"[{dm-t95*se:+.3f}, {dm+t95*se:+.3f}]", p_diff=2*stats.t.sf(abs(dm/se), J-1),
                          TOST_p_0p02=tost_p(dm, se, J, .02), TOST_p_0p03=tost_p(dm, se, J, .03), TOST_p_0p05=tost_p(dm, se, J, .05),
                          smallest_margin=max(abs(dm - t90*se), abs(dm + t90*se)), bootstrap_CI95_pooled=f"[{np.percentile(bs, 2.5):+.3f}, {np.percentile(bs, 97.5):+.3f}]"))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows_)

6.4 Clinical baselines and an interpretable-by-design model¶

Why. A 0.75 AUC is only meaningful relative to what a clinician already has. Total bilirubin alone has univariate AUC 0.70 (Table 1) — inside the CI of every model. We therefore add, all evaluated in the same nested protocol: (a) TB as a raw score (no fitting), (b) a single-marker LR on TB, (c) a four-variable LR chosen a priori on clinical grounds (TB, AST/Sgot, ALT/Sgpt, albumin), (d) the full LR plus the De Ritis ratio log(AST/ALT), and (e) an Explainable Boosting Machine without interactions (a GAM; the interpretable-by-design alternative to post-hoc explanation advocated by Rudin 2019) with a 12-candidate search.
Effect. Shows how much of the AUC is carried by one or two cheap tests and whether non-linear additive structure helps.
Advantage. The added value of the ten-variable models is stated against clinically meaningful comparators, and a model that needs no post-hoc XAI is available.
Trade-off. The EBM uses a small tuning grid; the four-variable set is not data-selected (selection from the same data would be optimistic).

In [16]:
from interpret.glassbox import ExplainableBoostingClassifier
def derive(Xd):
    Z = Xd.copy(); Z["logAST_ALT"] = np.log(Z.Sgot.clip(lower=1)/Z.Sgpt.clip(lower=1)); return Z
def pre_cols(logc, numc, catc=()):
    tr = []
    if logc: tr.append(("lg", Pipeline([("f", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one")), ("s", StandardScaler())]), list(logc)))
    if numc: tr.append(("num", StandardScaler(), list(numc)))
    if catc: tr.append(("cat", "passthrough", list(catc)))
    return ColumnTransformer(tr, verbose_feature_names_out=False)
SPECS = {
 "LR4":      dict(label="LR, 4 markers (TB, AST, ALT, albumin)", cols=["TB","Sgot","Sgpt","ALB"], mk=lambda: Pipeline([("pre", pre_cols(["TB","Sgot","Sgpt"], ["ALB"])), ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000))]), space={"clf__C": loguniform(1e-3, 1e2)}, n_iter=25),
 "LR1_TB":   dict(label="LR, total bilirubin only", cols=["TB"], mk=lambda: Pipeline([("pre", pre_cols(["TB"], [])), ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000))]), space={"clf__C": loguniform(1e-3, 1e2)}, n_iter=25),

def outer_gen(sp, rep, fold, tr, te, cands, seed):
    Xd = derive(X)[sp["cols"]]; Xtr, ytr = Xd.iloc[tr], y.iloc[tr]
    inner = list(StratifiedKFold(CFG["inner_splits"], shuffle=True, random_state=seed).split(Xtr, ytr)); ca, co = [], []
    for prm in cands:
        oof = np.zeros(len(ytr)); aucs = []
        for a, b in inner:
            mm = sp["mk"]().set_params(**prm).fit(Xtr.iloc[a], ytr.iloc[a]); pb = mm.predict_proba(Xtr.iloc[b])[:, 1]; oof[b] = pb; aucs.append(roc_auc_score(ytr.iloc[b], pb))
        ca.append(np.mean(aucs)); co.append(oof)
    best = int(np.argmax(ca)); thr = select_threshold(ytr.values, co[best]); platt = fit_platt(co[best], ytr.values)
    final = sp["mk"]().set_params(**cands[best]).fit(Xtr, ytr); p = final.predict_proba(Xd.iloc[te])[:, 1]; pc = platt.predict_proba(_logit(p))[:, 1]
    return dict(rep=rep, fold=fold, te=te, p=p, pc=pc, thr=thr, best=best, params=cands[best], inner_auc=ca[best], cand_auc=np.array(ca))
def run_gen(name):
    sp = SPECS[name]; cands = list(ParameterSampler(sp["space"], n_iter=sp["n_iter"], random_state=SEED))
    outer = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=CFG["outer_splits"], n_repeats=CFG["outer_repeats"], random_state=SEED)
    jobs = [(i//CFG["outer_splits"], i % CFG["outer_splits"], tr, te) for i, (tr, te) in enumerate(outer.split(X, y))]
    return Parallel(n_jobs=CFG["n_jobs"])(delayed(outer_gen)(sp, r, f, tr, te, cands, SEED + 100*r + f) for r, f, tr, te in jobs)
CLIN = {k: cached(f"clin_{k}", lambda k=k: run_gen(k)) for k in SPECS}
FOLDS_CLIN = {k: fold_frame(v) for k, v in CLIN.items()}
outer_cv = list(RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=CFG["outer_splits"], n_repeats=CFG["outer_repeats"], random_state=SEED).split(X, y))
tb_f = pd.DataFrame([dict(AUC=roc_auc_score(y.iloc[te], X.TB.iloc[te]), PR_AUC=average_precision_score(y.iloc[te], X.TB.iloc[te])) for tr, te in outer_cv])
rows_c = []
def clin_row(label, f, is_model=True):
    dd = FOLDS_PRIM["LR"].AUC.values - f.AUC.values; J = len(dd); se = np.sqrt((1/J + .25)*dd.var(ddof=1)); t95 = stats.t.ppf(.975, J-1)
    r_ = dict(model=label, AUC="{:.3f} [{:.3f}, {:.3f}]".format(*nb_ci(f.AUC)), PR_AUC="{:.3f}".format(f.PR_AUC.mean()))
    r_["BalAcc"] = "{:.3f} [{:.3f}, {:.3f}]".format(*nb_ci(f.BalAcc)) if is_model else "—"; r_["ΔAUC (full LR − model), 95 % CI"] = f"{dd.mean():+.3f} [{dd.mean()-t95*se:+.3f}, {dd.mean()+t95*se:+.3f}]" if label != "LR, 10 variables (primary)" else "(reference)"; return r_
rows_c.append(clin_row("LR, 10 variables (primary)", FOLDS_PRIM["LR"])); rows_c.append(clin_row("ExtraTrees (primary)", FOLDS_PRIM["ET"]))
for k in ["EBM", "LR_ratio", "LR4", "LR1_TB"]: rows_c.append(clin_row(SPECS[k]["label"], FOLDS_CLIN[k]))
rows_c.append(clin_row("Total bilirubin as a raw score (no fitting)", tb_f, False))
CLIN_TAB = pd.DataFrame(rows_c).set_index("model"); CLIN_TAB.to_csv(TAB/"table_clinical_baselines.csv"); CLIN_TAB

6.5 Operating points — sensitivity at fixed specificity, and accuracy at 0.5 versus the tuned threshold¶

Why. A Youden-type threshold (sensitivity ≈ 0.55) is a poor operating point whenever a missed diagnosis is costly, and accuracy at a tuned threshold is not comparable with the accuracy at 0.5 reported in most ILPD papers. We therefore report (i) sensitivity at fixed specificity 0.80/0.90 and specificity at fixed sensitivity 0.90/0.95 (read from the pooled out-of-fold ROC, bootstrap CIs) and (ii) accuracy, sensitivity and specificity at the conventional 0.5 cut-off next to the tuned-threshold accuracy.
Effect/Advantage. Lets the reader choose an operating point for their own cost ratio and compare with the literature on a like-for-like basis.

In [17]:
def sens_at_spec(yy, p, s): fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(yy, p); return float(np.interp(1-s, fpr, tpr))
def spec_at_sens(yy, p, s): fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(yy, p); return float(1 - np.interp(s, tpr, fpr))
yv = y.values; op = []
for m in ["LR", "ET", "SVM", "XGB"]:
    pb = POOL[m][0].mean(0); r_ = dict(model=m)
    for s_ in (0.80, 0.90):
        v = sens_at_spec(yv, pb, s_); bs = [sens_at_spec(yv[i], pb[i], s_) for i in BI[:500]]; r_[f"Sens @ Spec {s_:.2f}"] = f"{v:.2f} [{np.percentile(bs, 2.5):.2f}, {np.percentile(bs, 97.5):.2f}]"
    for s_ in (0.90, 0.95):
        v = spec_at_sens(yv, pb, s_); bs = [spec_at_sens(yv[i], pb[i], s_) for i in BI[:500]]; r_[f"Spec @ Sens {s_:.2f}"] = f"{v:.2f} [{np.percentile(bs, 2.5):.2f}, {np.percentile(bs, 97.5):.2f}]"
    r_["Acc @ 0.5"] = np.mean([np.mean((p >= .5) == yv) for p in POOL[m][0]]); r_["Sens @ 0.5"] = np.mean([((p >= .5) & (yv == 1)).sum()/(yv == 1).sum() for p in POOL[m][0]]); r_["Spec @ 0.5"] = np.mean([((p < .5) & (yv == 0)).sum()/(yv == 0).sum() for p in POOL[m][0]])
    r_["Acc @ tuned thr"] = FOLDS_PRIM[m].Acc.mean(); op.append(r_)

6.6 Leakage replication — can pre-split resampling reproduce the very high accuracies reported for ILPD?¶

Why. Several ILPD papers report accuracies of 85–95 %. We suspect that part of this comes from procedures that let information leak between training and test data, but a suspicion is not a finding. Here the suspicion is tested on our own data: the identical learners (default hyper-parameters, repeated 10-fold CV, threshold 0.5, the convention of that literature) are evaluated (A–C) with leakage-free, in-fold procedures and (D–G) with the leaky procedures — SMOTE or SMOTE-ENN applied to the whole data set before cross-validation, and exact duplicates left in the data.
Effect. If D–G reach accuracies in the 85–95 % range while A–C stay near 0.65–0.72, then such values are attainable by the procedure alone and cannot, without code inspection, be read as evidence of better models. We do not claim that any specific paper used these procedures.
Advantage. Converts a literature criticism into a reproducible experiment.

In [18]:
from imblearn.combine import SMOTEENN
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE
def prep_all(df_):
    Z = df_[FEATURES].copy(); Z[LOG_COLS] = np.log1p(Z[LOG_COLS]); cs = NUM_COLS + LOG_COLS; Z[cs] = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Z[cs]); return Z
dup = stage1.reset_index(drop=True).copy(); dup["Gender"] = (dup.Gender == "Male").astype(int); dup["target"] = (dup.target == 1).astype(int)
CLF = {"LR": lambda: LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000), "SVM": lambda: SVC(probability=True, random_state=SEED),
       "RF": lambda: RandomForestClassifier(300, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=1), "ET": lambda: ExtraTreesClassifier(300, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=1)}
def met05(yt, p):
    pr = (p >= .5).astype(int); tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(yt, pr, labels=[0, 1]).ravel(); return dict(Acc=(tp+tn)/len(yt), AUC=roc_auc_score(yt, p), Sens=tp/(tp+fn), Spec=tn/(tn+fp))
def leak_folds(ya): return list(RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=10, n_repeats=3, random_state=SEED).split(np.zeros(len(ya)), ya))
def scen_correct(df_, cn, resample=None):
    Xr, yr = df_[FEATURES].copy(), df_.target.values; rows_ = []
    for tr, te in leak_folds(yr):
        pre = make_pre(True).fit(Xr.iloc[tr]); Ztr, Zte = pre.transform(Xr.iloc[tr]), pre.transform(Xr.iloc[te]); ytr = yr[tr]
        if resample == "smote": Ztr, ytr = SMOTENC(categorical_features=[9], random_state=SEED).fit_resample(Ztr, ytr)
        if resample == "smoteenn": Ztr, ytr = SMOTEENN(random_state=SEED).fit_resample(Ztr, ytr)
        rows_.append(met05(yr[te], CLF[cn]().fit(Ztr, ytr).predict_proba(Zte)[:, 1]))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows_).mean().to_dict()
def scen_leaky(df_, cn, resample):
    Z, yr = prep_all(df_).values, df_.target.values
    Zr, yrr = (SMOTE(random_state=SEED).fit_resample(Z, yr) if resample == "smote" else SMOTEENN(random_state=SEED).fit_resample(Z, yr))
    rows_ = [met05(yrr[te], CLF[cn]().fit(Zr[tr], yrr[tr]).predict_proba(Zr[te])[:, 1]) for tr, te in leak_folds(yrr)]; return pd.DataFrame(rows_).mean().to_dict()
def scen_dups(df_, cn):
    Z, yr = prep_all(df_).values, df_.target.values
    rows_ = [met05(yr[te], CLF[cn]().fit(Z[tr], yr[tr]).predict_proba(Z[te])[:, 1]) for tr, te in leak_folds(yr)]; return pd.DataFrame(rows_).mean().to_dict()
def run_leak():
    rows_ = []
    for cn in CLF:
        for lab, fn in [("A. correct: de-duplicated, in-fold scaling, no resampling", lambda: scen_correct(d, cn)), ("B. correct: in-fold SMOTE-NC (training folds only)", lambda: scen_correct(d, cn, "smote")),
                        ("C. correct: in-fold SMOTE-ENN (training folds only)", lambda: scen_correct(d, cn, "smoteenn")), ("D. LEAK: SMOTE on whole data, then CV", lambda: scen_leaky(d, cn, "smote")),
                        ("E. LEAK: SMOTE-ENN on whole data, then CV", lambda: scen_leaky(d, cn, "smoteenn")), ("F. LEAK: 13 exact duplicates retained", lambda: scen_dups(dup, cn)),
                        ("G. LEAK: duplicates retained + SMOTE-ENN on whole data", lambda: scen_leaky(dup, cn, "smoteenn"))]:
            rows_.append(dict(model=cn, scenario=lab, **fn()))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows_)
LEAK = cached("leakage", run_leak); LEAK_TAB = LEAK.round(3); LEAK_TAB.to_csv(TAB/"table_leakage_replication.csv", index=False)

7. Results II — calibration, clinical utility and subgroup fairness¶

7.1 Calibration — with intervals, and a diagnosis of the recalibration design¶

Why. TRIPOD+AI requires calibration. A first version of this analysis recalibrated each fold with a Platt scaler fitted on the 3-fold inner out-of-fold predictions of models trained on 67 % of the outer-training data, and then applied it to a model refitted on 100 % of it. That train/apply mismatch is a known cause of calibration slopes ≠ 1: the inner models are more strongly shrunk than the refitted model, so the scaler over-corrects. It produced a slope of 0.80 for LR (over-confident) and 0.50 for the SVM — which flagged a design problem, not a property of the learners. Two further issues: (i) hyper-parameters are tuned on AUC, which is insensitive to the scale of the scores, so strongly regularised LR/ET are systematically under-confident before recalibration; (ii) SVC(probability=True) stacks its own internal Platt step under ours.
What is done. (a) The SVM score is now sigmoid(decision_function) with a single Platt step (§3.1). (b) The scaler and the threshold are fitted on 10-fold cross-fitted predictions of the selected configuration (training fraction 90 %), shrinking the mismatch. (c) The table reports, with 95 % patient-level bootstrap CIs, the calibration slope and calibration-in-the-large (CITL) for raw, Platt with K = 3 (old design) and Platt with K = 10 (current), and reliability curves are shown.
Effect. Slope and CITL close to 1 and 0 with intervals that can be judged; a visible demonstration of the mismatch.
Advantage. The calibration claims are now made with uncertainty and the design weakness is documented, not hidden.

In [19]:
from scipy.special import expit
def slope_citl(yy, p):
    pp = np.clip(p, 1e-6, 1-1e-6); z = np.log(pp/(1-pp)); a, b = 0.0, 1.0
    for _ in range(30):                                    # Newton–Raphson for the 2-parameter logistic recalibration model
        mu = expit(a + b*z); w = mu*(1-mu) + 1e-12; g = np.array([(yy-mu).sum(), ((yy-mu)*z).sum()])
        H = np.array([[w.sum(), (w*z).sum()], [(w*z).sum(), (w*z*z).sum()]]); st = np.linalg.solve(H + 1e-9*np.eye(2), g); a, b = a + st[0], b + st[1]
        if np.abs(st).max() < 1e-8: break
    return b, float(yy.mean() - pp.mean())
def recal_variant(name, res, K):
    # re-derive threshold + Platt calibrator with K-fold cross-fitting (K = 3 reproduces the old design); predictions p are unchanged
    def one(r):
        te = r["te"]; tr = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(n), te); Xtr, ytr = X.iloc[tr], y.iloc[tr]; seed = SEED + 100*r["rep"] + r["fold"]; oof = np.zeros(len(ytr))
        for a, b in StratifiedKFold(K, shuffle=True, random_state=seed + 1).split(Xtr, ytr):
            oof[b] = pipe_for(name).set_params(**r["params"]).fit(Xtr.iloc[a], ytr.iloc[a]).predict_proba(Xtr.iloc[b])[:, 1]
        pl = fit_platt(oof, ytr.values); return pl.predict_proba(_logit(r["p"]))[:, 1]
    out = Parallel(n_jobs=CFG["n_jobs"])(delayed(one)(r) for r in res); PC = np.zeros((3, n))
    for r, pc in zip(res, out): PC[r["rep"], r["te"]] = pc
    return PC
def cal_ci(P, B_=1000):
    pt = np.mean([slope_citl(y.values, p) for p in P], axis=0); r_ = np.random.default_rng(SEED); bs = []
    for _ in range(B_):
        i = r_.integers(0, n, n); bs.append(np.mean([slope_citl(y.values[i], p[i]) for p in P], axis=0)[0])
    lo, hi = np.percentile(bs, [2.5, 97.5]); return pt[0], lo, hi, pt[1], np.mean([brier_score_loss(y, p) for p in P])
PC3 = {m: cached(f"recal3_{m}", lambda m=m: recal_variant(m, NESTED[m], 3)) for m in MODELS}
cal_rows = []
for m in MODELS:
    for lab, P in [("raw score", POOL[m][0]), ("Platt, K = 3 (old design)", PC3[m]), ("Platt, K = 10 (current)", POOL[m][1])]:
        s_, lo, hi, ci_, br = cal_ci(P); cal_rows.append(dict(model=m, calibration=lab, slope=s_, slope_CI=f"[{lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f}]", CITL=ci_, Brier=br))
CAL = pd.DataFrame(cal_rows).set_index(["model", "calibration"]).round(3); CAL.to_csv(TAB/"table4_calibration.csv")

    p = P.mean(0); q = pd.qcut(p, nb, duplicates="drop"); g = pd.DataFrame({"p": p, "y": y.values}).groupby(q, observed=True).agg(p=("p", "mean"), y=("y", "mean"), n=("y", "size"))
    se = np.sqrt(g.y*(1-g.y)/g.n); a.errorbar(g.p, g.y, yerr=1.96*se, fmt="o-", color=col, label=lab, ms=4, lw=1.5, capsize=2)

7.2 Decision-curve analysis (clinical utility)¶

Why. AUC says nothing about whether using the model improves decisions. Net benefit weighs true positives against false positives at a clinician's risk threshold pt: NB = TP/n − FP/n · pt/(1−pt).
Effect. At 71 % prevalence "treat everyone" is a strong competitor; the model is only useful where its curve lies above both "treat all" and "treat none".
Advantage. Honest statement of where (if anywhere) the model adds value — reviewers in clinical journals expect it.

In [20]:
pts = np.arange(0.10, 0.91, 0.01)
def net_benefit(yv, p, pt):
    pred = p >= pt; tp = np.sum(pred & (yv==1)); fp = np.sum(pred & (yv==0)); return tp/len(yv) - fp/len(yv) * pt/(1-pt)
def nb_curve(m): return np.array([np.mean([net_benefit(y.values, p, pt) for p in POOL[m][1]]) for pt in pts])
nb_all = np.array([prev - (1-prev) * pt/(1-pt) for pt in pts])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2))

7.2b Is the decision-curve result an artefact of the 71 % prevalence? (prior-shift sensitivity)¶

Why. Net benefit, "treat all" and the calibrated probabilities are all prevalence-dependent. When the threshold probability pt is below the prevalence, "treat all" has net benefit prevalence − (1 − prevalence)·pt/(1 − pt) and is very hard to beat; this is largely a property of a 71 % referral population, not of the model. To show how the conclusion would look in a setting with fewer diseased patients we re-compute net benefit after a prior shift: the model's odds are multiplied by [π*/(1−π*)]/[π/(1−π)] and the net benefit is evaluated at the assumed prevalence π* (20 % and 5 %), holding sensitivity and specificity at each decision rule fixed (i.e. assuming the case-mix of cases and non-cases is unchanged).
Caveat. This is an illustration of prevalence dependence, not a validation: the non-liver class here is "other referred patients", not healthy people, so specificity in a true screening population would differ, and nothing in these data supports transporting the model to such a setting.
Effect/Advantage. Separates what is a property of prevalence from what is a property of the model, and justifies framing the work as diagnostic triage in a referral setting.

In [21]:
pts2 = np.arange(0.02, 0.91, 0.01); P_lr = POOL["LR"][1]; P_et = POOL["ET"][1]
def nb_shift(P, prev_new, pts_):
    prev0 = float(y.mean()); k = (prev_new/(1-prev_new))/(prev0/(1-prev0)); out = []
    for pt in pts_:
        o = pt/(1-pt)/k; t_orig = o/(1+o); nbs = []
        for p in P:
            tr_ = p >= t_orig; tpr = (tr_ & (y.values == 1)).sum()/(y.values == 1).sum(); fpr = (tr_ & (y.values == 0)).sum()/(y.values == 0).sum(); nbs.append(prev_new*tpr - (1-prev_new)*fpr*pt/(1-pt))
        out.append(np.mean(nbs))
    return np.array(out)

7.3 Subgroup performance (sex and age)¶

Why. ILPD is 76 % male and ≥ 60-year-olds are few; a model that works on average may fail in a subgroup (fairness / TRIPOD+AI item 13).
Effect. Subgroup AUCs with patient-level bootstrap CIs expose any disparity; overlapping CIs mean "no detectable difference", not "equal".
Advantage. Early warning against deploying a model that under-serves women or the elderly.

7.3b Formal inference for the subgroup differences¶

Why. Non-overlapping confidence intervals are not a hypothesis test, and four or more subgroup comparisons need multiplicity control. We therefore (i) report n and events per subgroup, (ii) test AUC differences with a two-sample patient-level bootstrap (Holm-adjusted over the four contrasts), (iii) test effect modification directly: a likelihood-ratio test of all nine sex × marker interactions in an unpenalised logistic model, and of the model score × sex, and (iv) examine the obvious clinical alternative — sex-specific reference ranges for bilirubin and enzymes — by z-scoring each laboratory value within sex (training-fold statistics only) and re-running the nested LR.
Effect. Separates "lower AUC in women" (a statement about discrimination, which depends on case mix) from "different marker–outcome relationships in women" (effect modification).
Advantage. The subgroup finding is reported with the strength of evidence it actually has.

def boot_diff(m1, m2, p, B_=2000):
    i1, i2 = np.where(m1)[0], np.where(m2)[0]; out = []; r_ = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    for _ in range(B_):
        a = r_.choice(i1, len(i1)); b = r_.choice(i2, len(i2))
        if len(set(yv[a])) == 2 and len(set(yv[b])) == 2: out.append(roc_auc_score(yv[a], p[a]) - roc_auc_score(yv[b], p[b]))
    out = np.array(out); d0 = roc_auc_score(yv[i1], p[i1]) - roc_auc_score(yv[i2], p[i2]); return d0, np.percentile(out, 2.5), np.percentile(out, 97.5), min(1, 2*min((out <= 0).mean(), (out >= 0).mean()))

    for (lab, a, b), r, pa in zip(CONTR, rs_, ph): sg.append(dict(model=nm, contrast=lab, dAUC=r[0], CI95=f"[{r[1]:+.3f}, {r[2]:+.3f}]", p_bootstrap=r[3], p_Holm=pa))

def sexnorm_nested():
    outer = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=3, random_state=SEED); P_ = np.zeros((3, n)); C_ = list(loguniform(1e-3, 1e2).rvs(25, random_state=SEED)); cols = LOG_COLS + NUM_COLS
    for i, (tr, te) in enumerate(outer.split(X, y)):
        Lg = X.copy().astype(float); Lg[LOG_COLS] = np.log1p(Lg[LOG_COLS]); Zq = Lg.copy()
        for s_ in (0, 1):
            trm = Lg.iloc[tr][Lg.Gender.iloc[tr] == s_][cols]; msk = (Lg.Gender == s_).values; Zq.loc[msk, cols] = (Lg.loc[msk, cols] - trm.mean())/trm.std()
        inner = list(StratifiedKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED + i).split(tr, y.iloc[tr])); best, bs_ = None, -1
        for c in C_:
            au = [roc_auc_score(y.iloc[tr[b]], LogisticRegression(C=c, max_iter=5000).fit(Zq.iloc[tr[a]], y.iloc[tr[a]]).predict_proba(Zq.iloc[tr[b]])[:, 1]) for a, b in inner]
            if np.mean(au) > bs_: bs_, best = np.mean(au), c
        P_[i//5, te] = LogisticRegression(C=best, max_iter=5000).fit(Zq.iloc[tr], y.iloc[tr]).predict_proba(Zq.iloc[te])[:, 1]
    return P_

7.4 The final model, and was the sample large enough? (TRIPOD+AI items 10 and 16)¶

Why. TRIPOD+AI requires the final model to be reported in a form that can be applied, and a justification of the sample size. We report the unpenalised logistic model fitted on all 566 patients (odds ratio per SD of each standardised, log-transformed marker, with 95 % CI and the equation in raw units), its bootstrap optimism-corrected calibration slope and AUC (Harrell, 300 resamples), and the sample size required by the Riley et al. (2020) criteria for 10 candidate parameters, a prevalence of 0.714 and an anticipated C-statistic of 0.75 (Cox–Snell R² obtained by simulation from the anticipated C and prevalence).
Effect. If n = 566 is below the required sample size, a calibration slope < 1 is expected, which is exactly what is observed.
Advantage. The reader can apply the model, and sees that the small-sample shrinkage is predictable rather than mysterious.

def boot_opt(B_=300):
    r_ = np.random.default_rng(SEED); Xa = sm.add_constant(Zs[FEATURES]); apparent = roc_auc_score(yv, Mf.predict(Xa)); oa, osl = [], []
    for _ in range(B_):
        i = r_.integers(0, n, n); Xb = sm.add_constant(Zs[FEATURES].iloc[i], has_constant="add")
        try: mb = sm.Logit(yv[i], Xb).fit(disp=0, maxiter=100)
        except Exception: continue
        po = mb.predict(Xa); oa.append(roc_auc_score(yv[i], mb.predict(Xb)) - roc_auc_score(yv, po)); osl.append(slope_citl(yv, po)[0])
    return dict(apparent_AUC=apparent, optimism_AUC=np.mean(oa), optimism_corrected_AUC=apparent - np.mean(oa), mean_calibration_slope_of_bootstrap_model_in_original_data=np.mean(osl))
BOPT = pd.Series(boot_opt()).round(4)
def cs_r2_from_c(C_target, prev, N=400000, seed=1):
    from scipy.optimize import brentq
    r_ = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    def auc_for(sig): yy = (r_.random(N) < prev).astype(int); return roc_auc_score(yy, r_.normal(yy*sig, 1))
    sig = brentq(lambda s_: auc_for(s_) - C_target, 0.05, 3.0, xtol=1e-3); yy = (r_.random(N) < prev).astype(int); z = r_.normal(yy*sig, 1)
    pp = LogisticRegression(C=1e6, max_iter=1000).fit(z.reshape(-1, 1), yy).predict_proba(z.reshape(-1, 1))[:, 1]
    ll1 = np.sum(yy*np.log(pp) + (1-yy)*np.log(1-pp)); ll0 = N*(prev*np.log(prev) + (1-prev)*np.log(1-prev)); return 1 - np.exp(2*(ll0 - ll1)/N), 1 - np.exp(2*ll0/N)
def riley(p_, r2, prev, mx, S=0.9, delta=0.05, marg=0.05):
    n1 = p_/((S-1)*np.log(1 - r2/S)); Sv = r2/(r2 + delta*mx); n2 = p_/((Sv-1)*np.log(1 - r2/Sv)); n3 = (1.96/marg)**2*prev*(1-prev)
    return {"n (shrinkage ≥ 0.9)": np.ceil(n1), "n (R² optimism ≤ 0.05)": np.ceil(n2), "n (risk precision ±0.05)": np.ceil(n3), "n required": np.ceil(max(n1, n2, n3))}
rows_r = []
for c_ in (0.75, 0.70):
    r2_, mx_ = cs_r2_from_c(c_, float(y.mean())); rows_r.append({"anticipated C": c_, "prevalence": round(float(y.mean()), 3), "R²_CS": round(r2_, 4), **riley(10, r2_, float(y.mean()), mx_), "n available": n})
RILEY = pd.DataFrame(rows_r).set_index("anticipated C"); RILEY.to_csv(TAB/"table11_riley_sample_size.csv")

8. Stability I — how much does performance depend on the data partition?¶

The original notebook reported one 80/20 split (AUC 0.83). We repeat the diagnostic for the study pipeline (200 random stratified 80/20 splits) so that the stability of a single-split estimate is quantified, and we locate the original split inside the resulting distribution. The SD of a hold-out AUC with n_test ≈ 113 is also predictable analytically (Hanley–McNeil), so the sweep is a check and a location device rather than a new finding.

Why. With n_test ≈ 113 the AUC of a single hold-out has an SD ≈ 0.04–0.05. A paper reporting only one split can be right by luck.
Effect. The distribution below is what a single split would report; the nested-CV mean should sit at its centre, and the original split's value is located in it.
Advantage. Justifies why nested repeated CV replaces the hold-out as the primary estimate, using the data themselves.

In [25]:
def _split_job(m, seed, tr, te):
    p = pipe_for(m, seed=seed).fit(X.iloc[tr], y.iloc[tr]); return roc_auc_score(y.iloc[te], p.predict_proba(X.iloc[te])[:, 1])
def run_split_sweep():
    sss = list(StratifiedShuffleSplit(n_splits=CFG["split_sweep"], test_size=0.2, random_state=0).split(X, y)); out = {}
    for m in ["LR", BEST_TREE]:
        out[m] = np.array(Parallel(n_jobs=CFG["n_jobs"])(delayed(_split_job)(m, SEED, tr, te) for tr, te in sss))
    tr0, te0 = train_test_split(np.arange(n), test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)      # the ORIGINAL notebook's split
    out["orig"] = {m: _split_job(m, SEED, tr0, te0) for m in ["LR", BEST_TREE]}; return out
SW = cached(f"splitsweep_{BEST_TREE}", run_split_sweep)

8.1 Stability II & III — hyper-parameters and decision threshold across outer folds¶

Why. If the "best" hyper-parameters or threshold change wildly from fold to fold, the final model is under-determined and any single tuned configuration should not be over-interpreted.
Effect. We report (a) the spread of the inner-search AUC across the 25 candidates — a flat landscape means hyper-parameters matter little; (b) the optimism gap (inner − outer AUC); (c) the dispersion of the chosen threshold.
Advantage. Separates "the model is robust" from "the tuning happened to land well".

9. Explainable AI (XAI)¶

9.0 Strategy — what is explained, on which data, and why this is more rigorous than a default SHAP plot¶

Decision Why Effect Advantage
Explain out-of-fold predictions (each patient explained by a model that never saw him/her; 5-fold × 3 repeats) explanations of training data describe over-fitting, not generalisable structure importances are slightly smaller/noisier than in-sample, but honest explanations are as trustworthy as the performance estimate
Two model classes: best tree ensemble (black box) and logistic regression (transparent benchmark) if both agree, the explanation reflects the data, not the learner a cross-model agreement test (§9.6) strongest argument for clinical plausibility
Three complementary methods: SHAP (model-internal attribution), permutation importance (performance-based), PDP/ICE (effect shape) each has different failure modes agreement across methods = robust finding no single-method artefact
Grouped permutation over clinical families (bilirubins, transaminases, protein/albumin) correlated features (VIF/ρ in §2.3) make single-feature permutation understate importance shows the family signal avoids the classic "correlated-feature masking" pitfall
Faithfulness (deletion) test an explanation is only useful if removing "important" features actually hurts the model AUC should fall faster when deleting SHAP-top features than random ones quantitative validity check rather than eyeballing

Hyper-parameters for the XAI models. Out-of-fold explanations (§9.1–9.5) use, in every outer fold, the model exactly as selected by the nested CV in that fold (same training patients, same hyper-parameters), so the explained models are the models whose performance is reported and no information from the held-out patients is used. A second configuration, tuned once on all 566 patients (FINAL), is used only where a single fitted model is unavoidable — PDP/ICE (§9.2) and the stability bootstraps (§10), which therefore condition on a tuned hyper-parameter set; no performance is claimed from it.

In [27]:
def tune_full(name):
    cands = list(ParameterSampler(SPACES[name], n_iter=CFG["n_iter"], random_state=SEED))
    if PRIMARY["imb"] != "smote": cands = [{k: v for k, v in c.items() if not k.startswith("smote__")} for c in cands]      # primary pipeline has no SMOTE step
    inner = list(StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED+7).split(X, y))
    def one(prm):
        oof = np.zeros(n); aucs = []
        for a, b in inner:
            m = pipe_for(name).set_params(**prm).fit(X.iloc[a], y.iloc[a]); pb = m.predict_proba(X.iloc[b])[:, 1]; oof[b] = pb; aucs.append(roc_auc_score(y.iloc[b], pb))
        return np.mean(aucs), oof
    res = Parallel(n_jobs=CFG["n_jobs"])(delayed(one)(p) for p in cands); sc = np.array([r[0] for r in res]); b = int(np.argmax(sc))
    return dict(params=cands[b], cv_auc=sc[b], thr=select_threshold(y.values, res[b][1]), cand_auc=sc)
FINAL = {m: cached(f"final_{m}", lambda m=m: tune_full(m)) for m in MODELS}
FIT = {m: pipe_for(m).set_params(**FINAL[m]["params"]).fit(X, y) for m in MODELS}      # fitted on all data (used only for PDP / local demos)

GROUPS = {"Bilirubin (TB, DB)": ["TB","DB"], "Transaminases (Sgpt, Sgot)": ["Sgpt","Sgot"], "Protein/albumin (TP, ALB, AG_ratio)": ["TP","ALB","AG_ratio"],

FGRP = {f: g for g, cols in GROUPS.items() for f in cols}
rho_in = {g: float(rho.loc[c, c].abs().values[np.triu_indices(len(c), 1)].max()) for g, c in GROUPS.items() if len(c) > 1}
print("Max |Spearman| inside each family:", {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in rho_in.items()})

def _norm_sv(sv):
    if isinstance(sv, list): sv = sv[1]
    sv = np.asarray(sv); return sv[:, :, 1] if sv.ndim == 3 else sv

def shap_values(pipe, name, Xexp, Xbg):
    # SHAP on the model's input space (after log/scale); units: probability for RF/ET, log-odds for the others
    pre, clf = pipe.named_steps["pre"], pipe.named_steps["clf"]; Z, Zb = pre.transform(Xexp), pre.transform(Xbg)
    if name == "LR": return _norm_sv(shap.LinearExplainer(clf, shap.maskers.Independent(Zb, max_samples=len(Zb))).shap_values(Z))
    return _norm_sv(shap.TreeExplainer(clf).shap_values(Z, check_additivity=False))

def perm_importance(pipe, Xte, yte, sets, n_rep, rng):
    base = roc_auc_score(yte, pipe.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]); out = {}
    for g, cols in sets.items():
        drops = []
        for _ in range(n_rep):
            perm = rng.permutation(len(Xte)); Xp = Xte.copy(); Xp[cols] = Xte[cols].values[perm]        # joint permutation keeps within-group correlation
            drops.append(base - roc_auc_score(yte, pipe.predict_proba(Xp)[:, 1]))
        out[g] = float(np.mean(drops))
    return out

def _roar_auc(name, params, seed, Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte, cols, med):
    # remove-and-retrain: the columns are set to their training median in BOTH train and test (a constant carries no information),
    # the model is re-fitted with the fold's selected hyper-parameters, and AUC is measured on the held-out fold
    Xa, Xb = Xtr.copy(), Xte.copy(); Xa[cols] = med[cols].values; Xb[cols] = med[cols].values
    return roc_auc_score(yte, pipe_for(name, seed=seed).set_params(**params).fit(Xa, ytr).predict_proba(Xb)[:, 1])

def _xai_fold(name, params, tr, te, seed, rep, n_perm, with_shap, deletion):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = X.iloc[tr], X.iloc[te], y.iloc[tr], y.iloc[te]
    pipe = pipe_for(name, seed=seed).set_params(**params).fit(Xtr, ytr)
    res = dict(te=te, rep=rep, pf=perm_importance(pipe, Xte, yte.values, {f: [f] for f in FEATURES}, n_perm, rng),
               pg=perm_importance(pipe, Xte, yte.values, GROUPS, n_perm, rng), sv=None, dele=[], roar=[])
    # reference for grouped importance: AUC drop when a RANDOM subset of the same size is permuted (controls the size confound of families)
    res["pr"] = {k: float(np.mean(list(perm_importance(pipe, Xte, yte.values, {i: list(rng.choice(FEATURES, k, replace=False)) for i in range(10)}, 1, rng).values()))) for k in (1, 2, 3)}
    if with_shap:
        sv = shap_values(pipe, name, Xte, Xtr); res["sv"] = sv
        if deletion:
            order = list(np.array(FEATURES)[np.argsort(-np.abs(sv).mean(0))]); med = Xtr.median()
            order_perm = [f for f, _ in sorted(res["pf"].items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])]
            uni = {f: max(roc_auc_score(ytr, Xtr[f]), 1 - roc_auc_score(ytr, Xtr[f])) for f in FEATURES}; order_uni = sorted(FEATURES, key=lambda f: -uni[f])
            base = roc_auc_score(yte, pipe.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]); res["dele"].append(dict(k=0, order="all", auc=base, draw=0))
            for k in range(1, 6):
                for oname, cols in [("SHAP-top first", order[:k]), ("SHAP-bottom first", order[::-1][:k]), ("Permutation-top first", order_perm[:k]), ("Univariate-AUC-top first", order_uni[:k])]:
                    Xm = Xte.copy(); Xm[cols] = med[cols].values; res["dele"].append(dict(k=k, order=oname, auc=roc_auc_score(yte, pipe.predict_proba(Xm)[:, 1]), draw=0))
                for dr in range(10):
                    cols = list(rng.choice(FEATURES, k, replace=False)); Xm = Xte.copy(); Xm[cols] = med[cols].values
                    res["dele"].append(dict(k=k, order="random", auc=roc_auc_score(yte, pipe.predict_proba(Xm)[:, 1]), draw=dr))
            for k in range(1, 6):                                                   # ROAR (remove-and-retrain) control
                for oname, cols in [("SHAP-top first", order[:k]), ("Permutation-top first", order_perm[:k]), ("Univariate-AUC-top first", order_uni[:k]), ("SHAP-bottom first", order[::-1][:k])]:
                    res["roar"].append(dict(k=k, order=oname, auc=_roar_auc(name, params, seed, Xtr, ytr.values, Xte, yte.values, cols, med), draw=0))
                for dr in range(5):
                    cols = list(rng.choice(FEATURES, k, replace=False)); res["roar"].append(dict(k=k, order="random", auc=_roar_auc(name, params, seed, Xtr, ytr.values, Xte, yte.values, cols, med), draw=dr))
    return res

def oof_explain(name, repeats, n_perm=5, with_shap=True, deletion=False):
    folds = sorted(NESTED[name], key=lambda r: (r["rep"], r["fold"]))[:5*repeats]          # the nested-CV outer folds and their selected hyper-parameters
    out = Parallel(n_jobs=CFG["n_jobs"])(delayed(_xai_fold)(name, r["params"], np.setdiff1d(np.arange(n), r["te"]), r["te"], SEED+i, r["rep"], n_perm, with_shap, deletion) for i, r in enumerate(folds))
    sv = None
    if with_shap:
        sv = np.zeros((repeats, n, len(FEATURES)))
        for o in out: sv[o["rep"], o["te"]] = o["sv"]
    return dict(sv=sv, pf=pd.DataFrame([o["pf"] for o in out]), pg=pd.DataFrame([o["pg"] for o in out]), pr=pd.DataFrame([o["pr"] for o in out]),
                dele=pd.DataFrame([dict(fold=i, **d) for i, o in enumerate(out) for d in o["dele"]]) if deletion else None,
                roar=pd.DataFrame([dict(fold=i, **d) for i, o in enumerate(out) for d in o["roar"]]) if deletion else None)

XPLAIN = {}
for m in MODELS:
    prim = m in (XP, "LR")
    XPLAIN[m] = cached(f"xai2_{m}_{XP}", lambda m=m, prim=prim: oof_explain(m, repeats=CFG["outer_repeats"] if prim else 2, n_perm=5 if not QUICK else 2,
                                                                               with_shap=(m != "SVM"), deletion=prim))
print("XAI computed for:", list(XPLAIN))

9.1 Global importance — SHAP vs permutation vs grouped permutation¶

Why. Three views of "which variables matter": SHAP (how much a variable moves the predicted risk), permutation (how much AUC is lost if the variable is scrambled), and grouped permutation (the same for a clinical family).
Effect. If the three agree, the ranking is not a by-product of the attribution method. Differences between single and grouped permutation expose correlated-feature masking.
Advantage. Triangulation instead of one pretty bar chart.
Trade-off. Permutation importance can be negative for irrelevant features (noise) — we show the sign rather than clipping it.

9.2 Direction and shape of effects — SHAP beeswarm, dependence plots and PDP/ICE¶

Why. Importance says how much; clinicians need which direction and where (thresholds, saturation). The beeswarm gives the direction, dependence plots show non-linear shape in clinical units, and ICE curves test whether the average effect (PDP) hides heterogeneity.
Effect. Face-validity check: higher bilirubin / ALP / transaminases should push risk up, higher albumin down.
Advantage. A model whose directions contradict medical knowledge would be a red flag even with a high AUC.

9.3 Local (patient-level) explanations¶

Why. Clinicians act on individual patients; a local explanation shows why this patient received this risk. Three archetypes are shown: a confidently-correct high-risk patient, a confidently-correct low-risk patient, and a false negative (a liver patient the model scored lowest) — errors are where explanations are most informative.
Effect. Reveals which features drive an error (e.g. normal enzymes in a patient with disease).
Advantage. Supports case-level review and clinician trust; SHAP values add up exactly to the model score minus the base value.

9.4 Faithfulness — deletion and remove-and-retrain (ROAR) tests, with competing rankings¶

Why. An explanation can look sensible and still not describe the model. A single deletion curve cannot establish faithfulness: (i) replacing features by the median without retraining produces out-of-distribution inputs, (ii) removing the whole top-ranked block (TB and DB) removes a whole signal block whatever ranking was used, and (iii) without a competing ranking any reasonable ordering (e.g. the univariate AUC of each marker) would probably pass the same test. The test therefore has four ingredients:
(a) Competing rankings: SHAP, permutation importance and univariate AUC (plus SHAP bottom-first and random removal as lower anchors); (b) two removal mechanisms — median replacement without retraining and ROAR (remove the features in training and test, retrain with the fold's selected hyper-parameters, re-evaluate), which avoids out-of-distribution inputs; (c) the baseline is the nested-CV outer-fold model (selected inside the fold, not tuned on all 566 patients); (d) the random-removal curve carries a band (range over 10 / 5 random draws).
Summary statistic. The area under the deletion curve (AUDC, mean out-of-fold AUC over k = 1…5 removed features): lower = the ordering identified more useful features. Paired differences between orderings use the Nadeau–Bengio interval over the 15 outer folds.
Effect / reading. A faithful explanation should beat random; it can only be claimed to be better than alternatives if it beats them. Ties with permutation importance are expected and are not a failure — both are legitimate rankings of the same model.
Caveats. Rankings are computed on the explained (held-out) fold, which is label-free for SHAP and the univariate ranking but label-using for permutation importance (this favours the competitor, i.e. is conservative for SHAP). Faithfulness to the model is not validity for the disease.

9.5 Cross-model agreement of explanations¶

Why. A finding that appears in only one learner may be an artefact of that learner. Agreement across six different model families (linear, bagging, boosting) is evidence that the data carry the signal.
Effect. Spearman correlations between importance vectors and Kendall's W (coefficient of concordance) summarise agreement.
Advantage. Turns "explanation stability" into a number that can be quoted in the manuscript. (SVM is included only through permutation importance, because exact SHAP for kernels is not tractable.)

def kendall_w(M):                             # M: items x raters (importance values) -> W in [0,1]
    R_ = M.rank(axis=0).values; nI, mR = R_.shape; S = ((R_.sum(1) - R_.sum(1).mean())**2).sum(); return 12*S/(mR**2*(nI**3 - nI))
