10. Stability II — explanation stability under training-data and algorithmic perturbation¶

10.0 What "stability" means here and how it is measured¶

A trustworthy explanation should not change materially when the training set is slightly different or when the learner's random seed changes. We measure four things, each for the primary tree model and for LR:

Facet Perturbation Metric Why it matters
Global rank stability 200 stratified bootstrap re-fits (tuned hyper-parameters fixed) mean pairwise Spearman ρ, Kendall's W, top-3 Jaccard would a different sample of hospital patients give a different "top features" list?
Importance uncertainty same 95 % percentile intervals of normalised importance, rank-frequency table gives error bars for the importance chart
Direction stability same % of replicates where the sign of (feature value ↔ SHAP) agrees with the majority protects against sign-flipping clinical interpretations
Local stability same, fixed set of 150 reference patients explained in every replicate mean pairwise cosine similarity of each patient's SHAP vector; top-1-feature agreement are individual explanations reproducible, not only the global average?
Algorithmic randomness 200 re-fits on the same data, only the random seed changes (and a 50-tree control) same metrics separates data-driven from seed-driven instability; seed invariance of a large fixed-hyper-parameter ensemble is nearly guaranteed, so a small-ensemble control shows when it is not
Milder perturbation 200 re-fits on random 80 % subsamples (no replacement) same metrics the bootstrap (≈ 63 % unique patients) is a harsher perturbation than drawing a fresh sample; the subsample brackets it from below
Null reference 100 bootstrap re-fits with permuted labels (no X–y association) same metrics defines what "no signal" looks like for the method; without it, "ρ = 0.76 is moderate" is just an adjective
Benchmark the same perturbations applied to logistic regression (SHAP of a linear model = standardised coefficient × deviation) same metrics a transparent model sets the attainable stability for these data; a fresh-sample reference from the simulation is in §12.2
Family level SHAP summed within the clinical families (additive, so shared credit between TB and DB cancels) mean pairwise ρ, Kendall W, frequency of the modal top family instability among correlated mid-ranked features does not contradict a stable family-level message

Reading the metrics. ρ, W and cosine are interpreted only against the null and benchmark rows, not against adjectives. The 150 reference patients are explained in every replicate; they are in the bootstrap sample in ≈ 63 % of replicates and out-of-bag in the rest (checked below).
Effect. High ρ / W / cosine relative to the null ⇒ explanations are reproducible and can be reported; low values ⇒ report them as hypotheses only.
Advantage. Few XAI papers quantify this; including it, with a reference scale, answers the most common reviewer criticism of SHAP-based studies ("explanations vary from run to run").

In [36]:
REF = np.sort(np.concatenate([np.random.default_rng(5).choice(np.where(y.values==c)[0], int(round(150*(y==c).mean())), replace=False) for c in (0, 1)]))
def _set_seed(pipe, name, s):
    if "smote" in pipe.named_steps: pipe.set_params(smote__random_state=s)
    if name in ("RF","ET","XGB","LGBM"): pipe.set_params(clf__random_state=s)
    if name == "CAT": pipe.set_params(clf__random_seed=s)
    return pipe
def _inbag(b):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 1000 + b); return np.concatenate([rng.choice(np.where(y.values==c)[0], (y==c).sum(), replace=True) for c in (0, 1)])
def _boot_job(name, b, mode):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 1000 + b); yy = y.values.copy(); oob = None
    if mode in ("bootstrap", "permuted"):
        idx = np.concatenate([rng.choice(np.where(yy==c)[0], (yy==c).sum(), replace=True) for c in (0, 1)]); oob = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(n), idx)
    elif mode == "subsample":                                     # 80 % of patients WITHOUT replacement: a milder perturbation than the bootstrap
        idx = np.sort(np.concatenate([rng.choice(np.where(yy==c)[0], int(round(.8*(yy==c).sum())), replace=False) for c in (0, 1)]))
    else:
        idx = np.arange(n)
    ytr = yy[idx]
    if mode == "permuted": ytr = rng.permutation(ytr)             # label-permutation NULL: the X-y association is destroyed, so any agreement left is a by-product of the method
    pipe = _set_seed(pipe_for(name).set_params(**FINAL[name]["params"]), name, 1000 + b)
    if mode == "seed50": pipe.set_params(clf__n_estimators=50)    # small-ensemble control: how much seed noise appears when the ensemble is NOT large?
    pipe.fit(X.iloc[idx], ytr); sv = shap_values(pipe, name, X.iloc[REF], X.iloc[idx])
    pi = perm_importance(pipe, X.iloc[oob], yy[oob], {f: [f] for f in FEATURES}, 3, rng) if mode == "bootstrap" else {}
    return sv, pi

def run_stability(name, mode):
    out = Parallel(n_jobs=CFG["n_jobs"])(delayed(_boot_job)(name, b, mode) for b in range(N_MODE[mode]))
    return dict(sv=np.array([o[0] for o in out]), pi=pd.DataFrame([o[1] for o in out]) if mode == "bootstrap" else None)

def stability_metrics(sv, Xref):
    B = sv.shape[0]; A = np.abs(sv).mean(1); I = A / A.sum(1, keepdims=True)                 # (B, p) normalised importance
    Rk = np.apply_along_axis(lambda r: stats.rankdata(-r), 1, I)                              # rank 1 = most important
    cc = np.corrcoef(Rk); iu = np.triu_indices(B, 1); rho_pair = cc[iu]
    top3 = [set(np.argsort(-r)[:3]) for r in I]; jac = np.array([len(top3[i] & top3[j])/len(top3[i] | top3[j]) for i, j in zip(*iu)])
    S = ((Rk.sum(0) - Rk.sum(0).mean())**2).sum(); W = 12*S/(B**2*(len(FEATURES)**3 - len(FEATURES)))
    # direction: sign of Spearman(feature value, SHAP) per replicate
    sg = np.array([[np.sign(stats.spearmanr(Xref[:, j], sv[b][:, j])[0]) for j in range(len(FEATURES))] for b in range(B)])
    maj = np.sign(sg.sum(0)); dir_agree = (sg == maj).mean(0)
    # local: cosine similarity of each reference patient's SHAP vector across replicates
    U = sv / (np.linalg.norm(sv, axis=2, keepdims=True) + 1e-12); cos = (np.linalg.norm(U.sum(0), axis=1)**2 - B) / (B*(B - 1))
    top1 = np.array([pd.Series(np.abs(sv[:, i]).argmax(1)).value_counts(normalize=True).iloc[0] for i in range(sv.shape[1])])
    return dict(I=I, Rk=Rk, rho_mean=rho_pair.mean(), rho_p05=np.percentile(rho_pair, 5), W=W, jac_top3=jac.mean(), dir_agree=dir_agree, dir_sign=maj,
                cos=cos, top1=top1)
SM = {k: stability_metrics(v["sv"], X.iloc[REF].values) for k, v in STAB.items()}
FAM = list(GROUPS)
def family_stability(sv):
    # SHAP values are additive, so the SHAP of a clinical family is the sum of its members' SHAP values (shared credit between TB and DB cancels out)
    G = np.stack([sv[:, :, [FEATURES.index(f) for f in GROUPS[g]]].sum(2) for g in FAM], axis=2); A = np.abs(G).mean(1); I = A / A.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    Rk = np.apply_along_axis(lambda r: stats.rankdata(-r), 1, I); B = len(Rk); iu = np.triu_indices(B, 1); rho = np.corrcoef(Rk)[iu].mean()
    S = ((Rk.sum(0) - Rk.sum(0).mean())**2).sum(); W = 12*S/(B**2*(len(FAM)**3 - len(FAM))); top = pd.Series(I.argmax(1)).value_counts(normalize=True)
    return dict(I=I, Rk=Rk, rho=rho, W=W, top_family=FAM[int(top.index[0])], top_freq=float(top.iloc[0]))
FS = {k: family_stability(v["sv"]) for k, v in STAB.items()}

                     family_level_Spearman=FS[(m, md_)]["rho"], family_level_W=FS[(m, md_)]["W"], top_family_modal_freq=FS[(m, md_)]["top_freq"]))

12. Do the conclusions generalise? Five further clinical datasets and a simulation with known ground truth¶

Why. Every substantive conclusion above — logistic regression is statistically hard to separate from tree ensembles, resampling adds nothing, nested-CV estimates are trustworthy, single hold-out splits are noisy, SHAP rankings are only moderately stable — comes from one 566-patient dataset. A single dataset cannot show that these are properties of small clinical tabular data rather than of ILPD. Two complementary checks are therefore added:

  1. §12.1 Five further small public clinical datasets (Pima diabetes, SAheart, Cleveland heart disease, BUPA liver disorders, Haberman survival; n = 303–768, event prevalence 26–51 %). The same leakage-free nested-CV design is applied (a lighter budget: 5 × 2 outer folds, 12 candidates per learner) to five learners, with and without SMOTE for LR and ET.
  2. §12.2 A simulation with known ground truth. Covariates are drawn from the real ILPD covariate distribution (smoothed bootstrap) and the outcome is generated from a known risk function (a linear logistic model, and a non-linear model with thresholds and an interaction), calibrated to the ILPD prevalence (71 %) and a population AUC of 0.75. Because the truth is known, we can measure whether nested CV is unbiased, whether the corrected-t intervals cover, how often TOST declares equivalence when it is (and is not) true, how noisy a single hold-out split is, and what level of explanation-rank agreement a fresh sample gives (the reference scale that was missing for the bootstrap audit in §10).

Effect. Findings that replicate are promoted from "observation on ILPD" to "pattern in small clinical tabular data"; findings that do not are reported as ILPD-specific.
Advantage. It converts the paper from a single-dataset case study into a multi-dataset study with a validated measurement instrument.
Trade-off. Five datasets and two simulated scenarios still do not make a benchmark; the budget is reduced (stated above) and the conclusions are worded accordingly.

12.1 Five additional clinical datasets (PMLB copies of public UCI / ESL data)¶

def load_ext(label):

EXT_MODELS = ["LR", "RF", "ET", "XGB", "SVM"]
EXT_NITER, EXT_OUTER = (3 if QUICK else 12), (5, 1 if QUICK else 2)
def ext_pipe(name, imb, ds, seed=SEED):
    num, cat = ds["num"], ds["cat"]
    pre = ColumnTransformer([("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("s", StandardScaler())]), num), ("cat", "passthrough", cat)])
    steps = [("pre", pre)]
    if imb == "smote":
        steps.append(("smote", SMOTENC(categorical_features=list(range(len(num), len(num)+len(cat))), k_neighbors=5, random_state=seed) if cat else SMOTE(k_neighbors=5, random_state=seed)))
    steps.append(("clf", build_clf(name, "none", seed))); return Pipeline(steps)

def _ext_fold(label, name, imb, i, tr, te, cands, seed):
    ds = EXT_DATA[label]; Xd, yd = ds["X"], ds["y"]; inner = list(StratifiedKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=seed).split(Xd.iloc[tr], yd[tr])); best, best_auc = 0, -1
    for j, prm in enumerate(cands):
        a_ = np.mean([roc_auc_score(yd[tr][b], ext_pipe(name, imb, ds, seed).set_params(**prm).fit(Xd.iloc[tr].iloc[a], yd[tr][a]).predict_proba(Xd.iloc[tr].iloc[b])[:, 1]) for a, b in inner])
        if a_ > best_auc: best, best_auc = j, a_
    p = ext_pipe(name, imb, ds, seed).set_params(**cands[best]).fit(Xd.iloc[tr], yd[tr]).predict_proba(Xd.iloc[te])[:, 1]
    return dict(fold=i, te=te, p=p, AUC=roc_auc_score(yd[te], p), Brier=brier_score_loss(yd[te], p), inner=best_auc)

def ext_nested(label, name, imb):
    ds = EXT_DATA[label]; cands = list(ParameterSampler(SPACES[name], n_iter=EXT_NITER, random_state=SEED))
    if imb != "smote": cands = [{k: v for k, v in c.items() if not k.startswith("smote__")} for c in cands]
    elif name in ("RF", "ET", "XGB", "SVM", "LR"): pass
    outer = list(RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=EXT_OUTER[0], n_repeats=EXT_OUTER[1], random_state=SEED).split(ds["X"], ds["y"]))
    return Parallel(n_jobs=CFG["n_jobs"])(delayed(_ext_fold)(label, name, imb, i, tr, te, cands, SEED + i) for i, (tr, te) in enumerate(outer))

EXT_RES = {}
for lab in EXT_SPECS:
    for m in EXT_MODELS: EXT_RES[(lab, m, "none")] = cached(f"extds_{lab.split()[0]}_{m}_none", lambda lab=lab, m=m: ext_nested(lab, m, "none"))
    for m in ("LR", "ET"): EXT_RES[(lab, m, "smote")] = cached(f"extds_{lab.split()[0]}_{m}_smote", lambda lab=lab, m=m: ext_nested(lab, m, "smote"))
def ext_auc(lab, m, imb="none"): return np.array([r["AUC"] for r in EXT_RES[(lab, m, imb)]])
def ext_brier(lab, m, imb="none"): return np.array([r["Brier"] for r in EXT_RES[(lab, m, imb)]])
rows = []
for lab in EXT_SPECS:

    rows.append(row)
EXT_AUC_TAB = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("dataset"); EXT_AUC_TAB.to_csv(TAB/"table_extdatasets_auc.csv"); EXT_AUC_TAB

# ---- learner parity (LR vs each learner) and the effect of SMOTE, per dataset, with Nadeau-Bengio intervals and TOST ----
def nb_delta(a, b, margin=.03):
    d_ = np.asarray(a) - np.asarray(b); J = len(d_); se = np.sqrt((1/J + .25)*d_.var(ddof=1)); dm = d_.mean(); t95, t90 = stats.t.ppf(.975, J-1), stats.t.ppf(.95, J-1)
    return dict(d=dm, se=se, lo=dm - t95*se, hi=dm + t95*se, p=2*stats.t.sf(abs(dm/se), J-1), tost=max(stats.t.sf((dm+margin)/se, J-1), stats.t.cdf((dm-margin)/se, J-1)), margin_min=max(abs(dm - t90*se), abs(dm + t90*se)))
par = []
for lab in EXT_SPECS:
    best_other = max([m for m in EXT_MODELS if m != "LR"], key=lambda m: ext_auc(lab, m).mean())
    for m in ("ET", "RF", "XGB", "SVM", best_other):
        r = nb_delta(ext_auc(lab, "LR"), ext_auc(lab, m)); par.append(dict(dataset=lab, comparison=f"LR − {m}" + (" (best non-LR)" if m == best_other and m not in ("ET", "RF", "XGB", "SVM") else ""), dAUC=r["d"], CI95=f"[{r['lo']:+.3f}, {r['hi']:+.3f}]", p=r["p"], TOST_p_0p03=r["tost"], smallest_margin=r["margin_min"], se=r["se"]))
EXT_PAR = pd.DataFrame(par).drop_duplicates(["dataset", "comparison"]).round(4)
sm_rows = []
for lab in EXT_SPECS:
    for m in ("LR", "ET"):
        r = nb_delta(ext_auc(lab, m, "smote"), ext_auc(lab, m, "none")); b_ = ext_brier(lab, m, "smote") - ext_brier(lab, m, "none")
        sm_rows.append(dict(dataset=lab, learner=m, dAUC_smote_minus_none=r["d"], CI95=f"[{r['lo']:+.3f}, {r['hi']:+.3f}]", p=r["p"], dBrier_smote_minus_none=b_.mean()))
EXT_SMOTE = pd.DataFrame(sm_rows).round(4); EXT_PAR.to_csv(TAB/"table_extdatasets_parity.csv", index=False); EXT_SMOTE.to_csv(TAB/"table_extdatasets_smote.csv", index=False)

# random-effects (DerSimonian-Laird) pooling over the five datasets of LR - ET, LR - best other, and SMOTE - none
def dl_pool(ds_, ses):
    ds_, ses = np.asarray(ds_), np.asarray(ses); w = 1/ses**2; fe = (w*ds_).sum()/w.sum(); Q = (w*(ds_-fe)**2).sum(); k = len(ds_)
    tau2 = max(0, (Q - (k-1))/(w.sum() - (w**2).sum()/w.sum())); wr = 1/(ses**2 + tau2); re = (wr*ds_).sum()/wr.sum(); se = np.sqrt(1/wr.sum())
    return re, se, tau2, 100*max(0, (Q-(k-1))/Q) if Q > 0 else 0

for lab_cmp, sel in [("LR − ET", lambda lab: nb_delta(ext_auc(lab, "LR"), ext_auc(lab, "ET"))),

                     ("LR − XGB", lambda lab: nb_delta(ext_auc(lab, "LR"), ext_auc(lab, "XGB"))),
                     ("LR − best non-LR", lambda lab: nb_delta(ext_auc(lab, "LR"), ext_auc(lab, max([m for m in EXT_MODELS if m != "LR"], key=lambda m: ext_auc(lab, m).mean())))),
                     ("SMOTE − none (LR)", lambda lab: nb_delta(ext_auc(lab, "LR", "smote"), ext_auc(lab, "LR", "none"))),
                     ("SMOTE − none (ET)", lambda lab: nb_delta(ext_auc(lab, "ET", "smote"), ext_auc(lab, "ET", "none")))]:
    rr = [sel(lab) for lab in EXT_SPECS]; re, se, tau2, I2 = dl_pool([r["d"] for r in rr], [r["se"] for r in rr])
    pool_rows.append(dict(contrast=lab_cmp, pooled_dAUC=re, CI95=f"[{re-1.96*se:+.3f}, {re+1.96*se:+.3f}]", tau=np.sqrt(tau2), I2_pct=I2, datasets_where_LR_within_0p03=int(sum(abs(r['d']) < .03 for r in rr)) if lab_cmp.startswith("LR") else np.nan))

12.2 Simulation with known ground truth¶

Design. Covariates: rows of the real, preprocessed ILPD matrix are resampled with replacement and numeric columns receive small Gaussian jitter (10 % of a SD) — a smoothed bootstrap that preserves the real skewness and the TB/DB, Sgpt/Sgot and ALB/AG collinearity. Outcome: y ~ Bernoulli(sigmoid(η(x))), where η is a known risk function with an intercept set to give the ILPD prevalence (71 %) and a scale set so that the population AUC of the true risk function is 0.75 (the level observed on ILPD). Two truths: S1 linear logistic (LR is correctly specified) and S2 non-linear (threshold effects for bilirubin, a Sgpt × Sgot interaction and a U-shaped age effect; tree ensembles can in principle exploit it). Replication: 50 independent datasets of n = 566 per scenario. Analysis per dataset: the same nested-CV protocol (5 outer folds, 3 inner folds, 8 random candidates; LR, ET, XGBoost), plus a 20 000-patient fresh test sample from the true model, on which the true AUC of every outer-fold model is measured.
Questions answered by the truth. (a) Is the nested-CV mean unbiased for the true AUC of the models it evaluates? (b) How large is the error of a single 20 % hold-out? (c) Does the 95 % Nadeau–Bengio interval for the mean AUC and for ΔAUC (LR − ET) cover the truth? (d) How often does TOST (margin ±0.03 and ±0.05) declare LR and ET equivalent, as a function of the true difference? (e) How well does SHAP recover the true importance order, and how stable are SHAP rankings across fresh samples (as opposed to bootstrap resamples of one dataset)?
Trade-off. The simulated covariate distribution is ILPD-like but the true risk function is our choice; the scenarios illustrate properties of the methods, not of liver disease.

from scipy.special import expit
def _norm_sv(sv):
    if isinstance(sv, list): sv = sv[1]
    sv = np.asarray(sv); return sv[:, :, 1] if sv.ndim == 3 else sv
_pre_all = make_pre(True).fit(X); _names = list(_pre_all.get_feature_names_out()); ZALL = pd.DataFrame(_pre_all.transform(X), columns=_names)[FEATURES]
Z_NUM = [c for c in FEATURES if c != "Gender"]
def draw_cov(m, rng):
    Zs = ZALL.iloc[rng.integers(0, len(ZALL), m)].reset_index(drop=True).copy(); Zs[Z_NUM] = Zs[Z_NUM] + rng.normal(0, .1, (m, len(Z_NUM))); return Zs
q = lambda c, p: float(np.quantile(ZALL[c], p))
def eta_raw(Zs, scen):
    g = lambda c: Zs[c].values
    if scen == "S1":      # linear: ILPD-like effect directions (bilirubin, enzymes, age up; albumin down; sex null)
        return .55*g("TB") + .55*g("DB") + .30*g("Alkphos") + .35*g("Sgpt") + .25*g("Sgot") - .30*g("ALB") - .10*g("AG_ratio") + .25*g("Age")
    hi = lambda c, p: (g(c) > q(c, p)).astype(float)       # S2: thresholds + interaction + U-shape (+ weaker linear terms)
    return 1.6*hi("TB", .6) + 1.1*hi("DB", .7) + .9*np.maximum(g("Sgpt"), 0)*np.maximum(g("Sgot"), 0) - .45*g("ALB") + .5*(g("Age") - .2)**2 + .25*g("Alkphos")
def _calibrate(scen, target_auc=.75, prev=.71, seed=123):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed); Zp = draw_cov(60000, rng); e0 = eta_raw(Zp, scen); e0 = (e0 - e0.mean())/e0.std()
    lo_, hi_ = .05, 6.0
    for _ in range(40):                                       # bisect the scale so that the population AUC is 0.75 (intercept re-solved for prevalence each time)
        c = (lo_ + hi_)/2; b0 = 0.0
        for __ in range(30): b0 += (prev - expit(b0 + c*e0).mean())/ (expit(b0 + c*e0)*(1-expit(b0 + c*e0))).mean()
        pr = expit(b0 + c*e0); yy = (np.random.default_rng(seed+1).random(len(pr)) < pr).astype(int); a_ = roc_auc_score(yy, pr)
        lo_, hi_ = (c, hi_) if a_ < target_auc else (lo_, c)
    return dict(c=c, b0=b0, mu=float(eraw_mu(scen, Zp)), sd=float(eraw_sd(scen, Zp)), auc=a_, prev=float(yy.mean()))
def eraw_mu(scen, Zp): return eta_raw(Zp, scen).mean()
def eraw_sd(scen, Zp): return eta_raw(Zp, scen).std()
SIM_CAL = {s: cached(f"sim_cal_{s}", lambda s=s: _calibrate(s)) for s in ("S1", "S2")}
def true_risk(Zs, scen): k = SIM_CAL[scen]; return expit(k["b0"] + k["c"]*(eta_raw(Zs, scen) - k["mu"])/k["sd"])
print({s: {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in d.items()} for s, d in SIM_CAL.items()})
POPZ = draw_cov(20000, np.random.default_rng(999)); POP_RISK = {s: true_risk(POPZ, s) for s in SIM_CAL}
POP_Y = {s: (np.random.default_rng(1000 + i).random(len(POPZ)) < POP_RISK[s]).astype(int) for i, s in enumerate(SIM_CAL)}
print("population AUC of the true risk function:", {s: round(roc_auc_score(POP_Y[s], POP_RISK[s]), 3) for s in SIM_CAL})
# true feature importance = AUC drop of the TRUE risk function when one feature is permuted (population-level)
def true_importance(scen):
    base = roc_auc_score(POP_Y[scen], POP_RISK[scen]); rng = np.random.default_rng(5); out = {}
    for f in FEATURES:
        Zp_ = POPZ.copy(); Zp_[f] = Zp_[f].values[rng.permutation(len(Zp_))]; out[f] = base - roc_auc_score(POP_Y[scen], true_risk(Zp_, scen))
    return pd.Series(out)
TRUE_IMP = {s: true_importance(s) for s in SIM_CAL}; pd.DataFrame(TRUE_IMP).round(3).T

SIM_N, SIM_REPS, SIM_NITER = 566, (6 if QUICK else 50), (3 if QUICK else 8)
def sim_pipe(name, seed): 
    clf = {"LR": LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000), "ET": ExtraTreesClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=seed, n_jobs=1),
           "XGB": XGBClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=seed, n_jobs=1, eval_metric="logloss")}[name]
    return Pipeline([("s", StandardScaler()), ("clf", clf)])
SIM_SPACES = {"LR": {"clf__C": loguniform(1e-3, 1e2)}, "ET": {"clf__max_depth": [3, 5, 8, None], "clf__min_samples_leaf": randint(1, 16), "clf__max_features": ["sqrt", 0.5, 1.0]},
              "XGB": {"clf__learning_rate": loguniform(.01, .2), "clf__max_depth": randint(2, 6), "clf__min_child_weight": randint(1, 11), "clf__subsample": uniform(.6, .4)}}
def sim_one(scen, rep):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(10_000*(1 if scen == "S1" else 2) + rep); Zs = draw_cov(SIM_N, rng); ys = (rng.random(SIM_N) < true_risk(Zs, scen)).astype(int); out = dict(scen=scen, rep=rep, prev=ys.mean())
    outer = list(StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=rep).split(Zs, ys)); res = {m: dict(auc=[], true=[]) for m in SIM_SPACES}
    for k, (tr, te) in enumerate(outer):
        inner = list(StratifiedKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=rep + 77*k).split(Zs.iloc[tr], ys[tr]))
        for m in SIM_SPACES:
            cands = list(ParameterSampler(SIM_SPACES[m], n_iter=SIM_NITER if m != "LR" else SIM_NITER, random_state=rep))
            sc = [np.mean([roc_auc_score(ys[tr][b], sim_pipe(m, rep).set_params(**c).fit(Zs.iloc[tr].iloc[a], ys[tr][a]).predict_proba(Zs.iloc[tr].iloc[b])[:, 1]) for a, b in inner]) for c in cands]
            fit = sim_pipe(m, rep).set_params(**cands[int(np.argmax(sc))]).fit(Zs.iloc[tr], ys[tr])
            res[m]["auc"].append(roc_auc_score(ys[te], fit.predict_proba(Zs.iloc[te])[:, 1])); res[m]["true"].append(roc_auc_score(POP_Y[scen], fit.predict_proba(POPZ)[:, 1]))
    out.update({f"{m}_{k}": np.array(v) for m, d in res.items() for k, v in d.items()})
    # explanation recovery + fresh-sample stability: fixed-hyper-parameter ET on the whole simulated dataset, SHAP on a COMMON reference set
    et = sim_pipe("ET", rep).set_params(clf__min_samples_leaf=5, clf__max_features="sqrt").fit(Zs, ys); ref = POPZ.iloc[:300]
    sv = _norm_sv(shap.TreeExplainer(et.named_steps["clf"]).shap_values(et.named_steps["s"].transform(ref), check_additivity=False)); out["shap_imp"] = np.abs(sv).mean(0)
    lr = sim_pipe("LR", rep).fit(Zs, ys); out["lr_imp"] = np.abs(lr.named_steps["clf"].coef_[0])
    return out
SIM = {s: cached(f"sim_{s}_{SIM_REPS}", lambda s=s: Parallel(n_jobs=CFG["n_jobs"])(delayed(sim_one)(s, r) for r in range(SIM_REPS))) for s in ("S1", "S2")}
print({s: len(v) for s, v in SIM.items()}, "simulated datasets per scenario")

# explanation recovery and stability across FRESH samples (the reference scale for the bootstrap audit in section 10)
def norm_imp(v): v = np.asarray(v, float); return v/v.sum()
srows = []
for s in ("S1", "S2"):
    R = SIM[s]; Ish = np.array([norm_imp(r["shap_imp"]) for r in R]); Ilr = np.array([norm_imp(r["lr_imp"]) for r in R]); ti = TRUE_IMP[s].reindex(FEATURES).values
    rec_sh = [stats.spearmanr(i_, ti)[0] for i_ in Ish]; rec_lr = [stats.spearmanr(i_, ti)[0] for i_ in Ilr]
    pw = lambda M: np.mean([stats.spearmanr(M[i], M[j])[0] for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(len(M)), 2)])
    Rk = np.apply_along_axis(lambda r: stats.rankdata(-r), 1, Ish); W = 12*((Rk.sum(0) - Rk.sum(0).mean())**2).sum()/(len(Rk)**2*(len(FEATURES)**3 - len(FEATURES)))
    top3 = [set(np.argsort(-r)[:3]) for r in Ish]; jac = np.mean([len(top3[i] & top3[j])/len(top3[i] | top3[j]) for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(len(top3)), 2)])
    srows.append(dict(scenario=s, SHAP_vs_truth_Spearman=np.mean(rec_sh), LRcoef_vs_truth_Spearman=np.mean(rec_lr), fresh_sample_pairwise_Spearman_SHAP_ET=pw(Ish), fresh_sample_pairwise_Spearman_LR_coef=pw(Ilr), fresh_sample_Kendall_W=W, fresh_sample_top3_Jaccard=jac))

ax[0].axhline(0, color=INK2, lw=.8); ax[0].set_xticks(range(3), ["LR", "ET", "XGB"]); ax[0].set_ylabel("nested-CV AUC − true AUC (per simulated dataset)"); ax[0].set_title("A  Is nested CV unbiased?"); ax[0].legend(fontsize=8)

13. Interpretation of the results¶

13.1 Findings, in the order a reader needs them¶

  1. Discrimination is moderate; parity with ExtraTrees is demonstrated, parity with the others is not. Nested-CV AUC is 0.749 (LR), 0.750 (ET), 0.739 (RF), 0.738 (CatBoost), 0.722 (XGBoost), 0.720 (LightGBM) and 0.685 (SVM) (Table 2, Fig. 4). No pairwise difference survives Holm correction (smallest adjusted p = 0.17, ET vs SVM). A Friedman test on the 15 fold AUCs gives χ² = 49.1 (p = 7 × 10⁻⁹), which is descriptive only because folds are dependent, and is driven largely by the SVM. A non-significant result is not equivalence: LR − ET has ΔAUC = −0.001 (CI −0.018 to +0.016; TOST p = 0.001 at ±0.03), so ET can be called equivalent within ±0.03. For RF and CatBoost the CI reaches +0.036/+0.037, so equivalence holds at ±0.05 only; for XGBoost and LightGBM (upper limits +0.056/+0.063) and the SVM (+0.005 to +0.123) it cannot be shown. Effect: "ExtraTrees is the best model" (the original conclusion) is not supported, and neither is "all learners are the same". Advantage: the transparent LR is not detectably worse than the ensembles at the ±0.03–0.05 level, which is the claim the data can carry.
  2. The boosting ranking is not a tuning-budget artefact. With 150 instead of 25 candidates, XGBoost changed by −0.007 (CI −0.028 to +0.013), LightGBM by 0.000 and CatBoost by −0.0002; the SVM with 100 candidates by +0.002. Inner-AUC optimism grew (0.009–0.021), as expected from a larger search on a flat landscape.
  3. Accuracy is not a valid headline metric here. At the tuned threshold accuracy is 0.62–0.64 (RBF-SVM 0.55), below the 0.714 obtained by calling everyone a liver patient. At the conventional 0.5 cut-off LR and ET reach 0.71 accuracy only because they label 97 % of liver patients and 92–93 % of non-liver patients positive (sensitivity 0.97, specificity 0.07–0.08). Both are reported so that results at the Youden threshold can be compared with literature values at 0.5. At fixed specificity 0.80 the LR sensitivity is 0.59 (0.52–0.67); at specificity 0.90 it is 0.51 (0.44–0.56); at 90 % sensitivity specificity is only 0.25.
  4. A single split is a lottery, and leakage can create published-looking accuracies. Over 200 random 80/20 splits the hold-out AUC has mean 0.754 (LR) / 0.751 (ET) and SD 0.041 / 0.039 (95 % of splits within 0.67–0.83); this SD is of the same order as the Hanley–McNeil standard error for n_test ≈ 113 (≈ 0.05), so the sweep adds a location of the original split (AUC 0.836 for LR, 98.5th percentile; 0.808 for ET, 93rd percentile) rather than a new fact. The leakage replication (§8.2) shows what such errors do on these data: applying SMOTE-ENN to all patients before cross-validation raises accuracy to 0.91 (LR), 0.94 (SVM), 0.95 (RF, ET) and AUC to 0.95–0.99, whereas the leakage-free pipeline gives 0.62–0.73 accuracy and AUC 0.72–0.75 (SVM without resampling 0.67). Plain SMOTE before splitting inflates AUC less for LR (0.77) but strongly for RF and ET (0.91–0.95). Retained exact duplicates add at most ≈ 0.02 AUC. This shows that leakage of this kind is sufficient to produce the 90–95 % accuracies reported in the ILPD literature; it does not show that any specific paper leaked.
  5. Imbalance handling is not what produces performance — with one exception. For six of seven learners SMOTE-NC changes AUC by ≤ 0.005 (all unadjusted p ≥ 0.76) and class weights by ≤ 0.008 (all p ≥ 0.30) (§6.2, tabulated for all seven learners). The exception is the RBF-SVM, whose AUC rises from 0.685 to 0.753 with SMOTE-NC and to 0.752 with class weights (p = 0.03 for each, unadjusted); without resampling its threshold is unstable (SD 0.30, range 0.07–0.75), so the SVM's apparent inferiority in the primary analysis is a property of an unweighted RBF-SVM on 71/29 data, not of the kernel as such. On the five external datasets SMOTE changes AUC by −0.002 (pooled CI −0.004 to +0.001) while the Brier score worsens in 8 of 10 learner-dataset pairs (by up to +0.047).
  6. Calibration is acceptable after cross-fitting; utility depends on prevalence. With the current design (Platt scaler fitted on 10-fold cross-fitted predictions) the calibration slope is 0.92 (0.72–1.16) for LR, 0.98 (0.77–1.24) for ET and 1.17 (0.85–1.57) for the SVM, with calibration-in-the-large ≈ 0 and Brier 0.173–0.174 vs 0.204 for the prevalence-only model. With the original K = 3 design the LR slope was 0.79 (0.62–0.99) and the SVM slope 1.77, which supports the explanation that a calibrator fitted on models trained on two thirds of the data does not match a model refitted on all training data; K = 10 reduces but, for LR, may not remove this mismatch. At the cohort's prevalence decision-curve analysis shows no net benefit over "treat everyone" for thresholds 0.2–0.5 (LR − treat-all −0.012 to 0.000) and clear benefit only at ≥ 0.6 (+0.056 at 0.6, +0.258 at 0.7). This is largely a consequence of 71 % prevalence. Re-weighting to hypothetical prevalences (constant sensitivity and specificity assumed) widens the range of useful thresholds to 0.10–0.74 at 20 % and 0.03–0.90 at 5 % for LR; this shows the mechanism and is not evidence that the model would be useful for screening.
  7. Sex differences in discrimination are real in this sample but not explained. AUC is 0.635 (0.543–0.724) in 138 women (90 liver patients, 48 non-liver) and 0.771 (0.723–0.813) in 428 men; the paired bootstrap difference is 0.136 (0.040–0.248; Holm p = 0.028 for LR, 0.048 for ET). AUC rises with age (≥ 60 vs < 40: +0.134, Holm p = 0.030 for LR; 0.063 for ET). No individual sex × marker interaction is significant (omnibus LRT p = 0.78); the model-score × sex slope difference (1.20 in women vs 2.12 in men) has p = 0.075. Sex-specific z-scoring of the laboratory values (a proxy for sex-specific reference ranges) raises the female AUC only from 0.634 to 0.649, so reference-range differences do not account for the gap in this analysis.
  8. Clinical baselines. Total bilirubin alone gives AUC 0.699 (0.637–0.761); the ten-variable LR improves on it by 0.050 (0.009–0.091) — a small but resolvable gain. A four-marker LR (TB, AST, ALT, albumin) reaches 0.739 (ΔAUC to full LR +0.010, −0.012 to +0.032), adding the De Ritis ratio changes nothing (0.750), and an interpretable-by-design EBM (GAM without interactions) reaches 0.743 (+0.006, −0.014 to +0.026). The simplest defensible clinical model is therefore a handful of liver tests; the extra variables add little. The final LR odds ratios (per SD, Table 10) are significant for ALT (1.90, 1.20–3.03), age (1.33), total protein (2.60) and albumin (0.27); the bilirubins have very wide intervals because TB and DB are almost collinear (ρ = 0.96).
  9. Sample size. The Riley et al. criteria for shrinkage ≥ 0.9 require n = 530 if the true C-statistic is 0.75 and n = 859 if it is 0.70; n = 566 is adequate only for the more optimistic case, consistent with the LR calibration slope of 0.92.
  10. Generalisation beyond ILPD. On five public clinical datasets (Pima, SAheart, Cleveland, BUPA liver, Haberman; 303–768 patients) the pooled LR − ET difference is −0.003 (−0.015 to +0.010; I² = 12 %), LR − best non-LR learner −0.008 (−0.021 to +0.006), and the LR point estimate is within 0.03 AUC of ET on four of five datasets. In the simulation (two scenarios, 50 datasets of n = 566, true AUC of the risk function 0.75) the nested-CV AUC bias is ≤ 0.004 for LR, ET and XGBoost, interval coverage 0.98–1.00, and the error of a single fold-level estimate has SD 0.046–0.051 — i.e. the corrected intervals are valid, slightly conservative, and single splits are as noisy as the ILPD sweep suggests. TOST at ±0.03 declared equivalence in 42 % (LR − ET, S1), 8 % (LR − XGBoost, S1), 24 % (S2) and 4 % (S2) of replicates although the true differences were within ±0.03 in 90–100 %: a study of this size has low power to prove parity, which is why §6.3 reports intervals rather than a verdict.

13.2 Explainability findings¶

  • What drives predictions. SHAP and permutation importance agree (ρ = 0.93), and so does a simple univariate-AUC ranking (ρ = 0.93), so agreement among them is expected and is not independent evidence of correctness. Bootstrap median SHAP shares for ExtraTrees are DB 17 % (95 % interval 12.7–21.0), TB 14 % (10.5–17.6), Sgpt 12 % (8.3–16.9), Sgot 12 % (8.3–16.3), Alkphos 11 % (6.4–14.9), Age 9 %, ALB 7 %, A/G 6 %, Gender 5 % and TP 4 %; the intervals of the first five overlap, so “dominated by bilirubin” is only supported at the family level (grouped permutation: bilirubin AUC drop 0.101, SE 0.006, vs 0.022 for two random features; transaminases 0.062; ALP 0.017). The protein/albumin family has a SHAP share of 13 % but a grouped permutation drop of 0.000, i.e. its information is redundant with other features. Direction of effect is stable for all features except sex (71 % sign agreement over replicates) and total protein (76 %); these two should not be interpreted.
  • Faithfulness is established against random removal, not against competing rankings. For ExtraTrees, deleting the SHAP-top features lowers the area under the deletion curve by 0.037 (CI 0.012–0.062) more than random removal and 0.050 (0.018–0.082) more than removing the SHAP-bottom features (median replacement); with remove-and-retrain (ROAR) the corresponding differences are 0.042 (0.016–0.067) and 0.054 (0.017–0.091). Permutation-top-first and univariate-AUC-top-first rankings are as good as SHAP (differences +0.002 to +0.009, all CIs including 0). For LR under ROAR no ranking differs detectably from random removal (SHAP vs random 0.028, CI −0.005 to +0.061), as expected when correlated features substitute for each other after retraining. Baseline AUCs here come from models tuned on all 566 patients and are mildly optimistic (0.744 for ET vs 0.750 nested).
  • Correlation matters. TB and DB are almost collinear (ρ = 0.96), so single-feature importances split their credit; family-level results are the interpretable ones.

13.3 Stability findings (the answer to "explain stability")¶

Level Result Interpretation
Data partition split-sweep SD 0.04, outer-fold SD 0.05–0.07 a single split carries ± 0.08 uncertainty → nested repeated CV is required
Hyper-parameters inner-AUC landscape SD ≈ 0.004–0.026; only 20–53 % of folds choose the same candidate; inner−outer optimism ≈ 0 for LR/RF/ET, 0.012 for XGB/LGBM, 0.020 for SVM many configurations perform equally; performance is stable although the chosen configuration is not; inner−outer ≈ 0 does not prove absence of optimism because inner models train on less data
Decision threshold SD 0.02–0.06 across folds for tree models and LR (SVM 0.30, range 0.07–0.75) the cut-off is the least stable component → report sensitivity/specificity at fixed specificity and recalibrate locally
Explanation — algorithmic seed ET mean rank-ρ 0.98 (0.95 with 50 trees) near-guaranteed for a large fixed-hyper-parameter ensemble; not a strong finding
Explanation — training-data perturbation ET bootstrap ρ = 0.764 (5th percentile 0.50), W = 0.765, top-3 Jaccard 0.52; label-permuted null 0.04; LR benchmark 0.846 (W 0.846, Jaccard 0.61); 80 % subsamples 0.92 (ET) / 0.94 (LR) far above the null, below the transparent LR benchmark; DB in the top three in 97.5 % of replicates, TB 75.5 %, Sgpt 43 %, Sgot 41 %, ALP 25.5 %
Explanation — family level ET ρ = 0.889 (W 0.889); the most frequent top family has frequency 94 % for ET (bilirubin) vs 62 % for LR the coarse structure is stable once correlated features are grouped
Explanation — local ET median per-patient cosine 0.81 (10th percentile 0.58), top-1 agreement 56 %; LR 0.96 (0.93), 77 % individual explanations from the tree ensemble are noticeably less reproducible than LR; the 150 reference patients were in-bag in 63 % (52–73 %) of bootstrap replicates
Explanation — model family / method mean ρ across 6 learners 0.68 (min 0.02, W 0.73); permutation 0.68 (W 0.72); SHAP vs permutation ρ 0.93 explanation agreement across learners is moderate, not high
Fresh-sample stability (simulation) SHAP ET mean ρ 0.61 across fresh samples (W 0.62, top-3 Jaccard 0.53–0.61); SHAP recovers the true importance order with ρ = 0.55–0.61 (LR coefficients 0.23–0.42) a bootstrap is a harsher perturbation than a fresh sample, but even fresh samples of n = 566 give only moderate rank stability

Overall. Performance and the family-level explanation (bilirubin and transaminases ≫ ALP/age ≫ protein/albumin, with ↑ risk for liver enzymes and ↓ for albumin) are robust; fine-grained rankings, the decision threshold, the identity of the tuned hyper-parameters and individual-patient attributions from tree ensembles are not. Because LR is equivalent to ET within ±0.03, matches the other ensembles within the margins above and gives more reproducible local explanations, we suggest LR as the primary clinical model, with ET and SHAP as a non-linear check. The RBF-SVM is discouraged (unstable threshold without resampling, no exact SHAP).

13.4 Suggested wording for the manuscript¶

"In repeated nested cross-validation (n = 566 referred patients) the AUC of logistic regression and ExtraTrees was 0.75 (95 % CI 0.68–0.82) and equivalent within ±0.03 (TOST p = 0.001); equivalence with the boosting models could not be shown. Resampling or class weighting did not change AUC for six of seven learners and worsened calibration on five external datasets. Net benefit over treating all patients was observed only at decision thresholds ≥ 0.6 at the cohort's prevalence; the model should not be read as a screening tool. Discrimination was lower in women (AUC 0.64 vs 0.77). SHAP explanations were faithful relative to random removal but not to competing rankings, and their ordering was moderately stable under bootstrap resampling (ρ = 0.76 vs a null of 0.04), with the bilirubin family consistently ranked first."

14. Limitations and threats to validity (to be copied into the Discussion)¶

  1. Single-source, retrospective, referral cohort (Andhra Pradesh, India; 71 % liver patients). The "non-liver" class consists of other referred patients, so specificity is against other patients, and recalibrated probabilities, thresholds and net benefit are tied to this prevalence and do not transport to screening or primary-care populations. No external or temporal validation was possible; nested CV estimates internal validity only.
  2. No patient identifier. Exact duplicates were removed, but repeated visits of one patient with different values cannot be excluded; residual clustering would make CV estimates mildly optimistic.
  3. Label definition. "Liver patient" vs "non-liver" is a coarse label, not a specific diagnosis.
  4. Small sample (n = 566; 162 minority-class cases). The Riley et al. criterion for shrinkage ≥ 0.9 is met only if the true C-statistic is ≈ 0.75 or higher (n required 530 vs 859 at C = 0.70); the LR calibration slope of 0.92 (CI 0.72–1.16) is consistent with mild overfitting.
  5. Equivalence claims are limited by power. LR–ET parity holds within ±0.03 AUC; for RF/CatBoost only within ±0.05; for XGBoost, LightGBM and the SVM parity could not be shown. Margins are conventions, not utility-derived. The Nadeau–Bengio correction was derived for random subsampling; its use with repeated k-fold CV is an accepted approximation. Folds from repeated CV are not independent, so the Friedman test is descriptive.
  6. Tuning. A random search with 25 candidates (150 for boosting, 100 for the SVM in the check) on a flat landscape selects configurations that are largely arbitrary; the larger searches did not change the conclusions, but Bayesian optimisation was not tried. Hyper-parameters used for the explanation analyses were tuned on all 566 patients, so the baseline AUCs there are mildly optimistic.
  7. Calibration design. Platt scaling and the threshold are fitted on cross-fitted predictions of models trained on 90 % (K = 10) of the outer-training data and applied to a model refitted on 100 %. K = 10 reduced the mismatch seen with K = 3 (LR slope 0.79 → 0.92) but does not remove it.
  8. Decision-curve analysis at the cohort prevalence shows net benefit only at thresholds ≥ 0.6. The prior-shift curves assume constant sensitivity and specificity and are illustrations of how prevalence changes net benefit, not validation in a screening population.
  9. Explanations. SHAP attributions are conditional on the model and are shared between correlated features; they describe model behaviour, not causal effects. The faithfulness tests show that SHAP beats random removal but not competing rankings; the deletion test with median replacement creates out-of-distribution inputs, which ROAR avoids at the cost of retraining. A bootstrap perturbs the data more than a fresh sample would (63 % unique patients); the simulation provides the fresh-sample reference. Seed invariance of a large fixed-hyper-parameter ensemble is near-guaranteed and is not evidence of robustness.
  10. Subgroups. Women (n = 138, 48 non-liver) and the age bands are small. The male-female AUC difference is significant after Holm adjustment for LR (p = 0.028) and borderline for ET (p = 0.048), but no sex × marker interaction is significant, so the mechanism is unexplained; sex-specific z-scoring did not close the gap.
  11. Generalisation. The five additional datasets are public benchmarks (PMLB copies) of different clinical problems, only one of them hepatic (BUPA); the simulation chooses its own true risk function. Both support, but cannot prove, that the ILPD findings are general.
  12. Leakage replication. It shows that SMOTE-ENN applied before splitting is sufficient to give 90–95 % accuracy on these data. It does not establish that any specific published study leaked; that would require its code.
